review.focus: At 12.Bxc6 you took material without checking what 11...Nxc3 attacked. Make a habit of asking what the opponent's last move threatens before capturing.

review.headline: An even Exchange QGD decided by one careless rook move

sections.text: A normal Exchange Queen's Gambit: 4.cxd5 exd5 5.Bg5 Nbd7 6.Qc2 c6 7.e3 Be7 8.Bd3. You tried to get active with 9...Qb6?!, which was slightly inaccurate, and 10...g5 followed 10.Nge2. After 11.Bg3 Nh5 12.O-O Nxg3 13.Nxg3 you had traded off White's bishop.

The middlegame went in cycles: 15.Nf5 Bxf5 16.Bxf5 Bd6, then 17.h3 Bh2+ 18.Kh1 Bd6, which just moved the bishop out and back. 19.e4 dxe4 and the trades with 21.Bxe4 Nxe4 22.Rxe4 left the position about equal.
You kept it level through 23...Rxe4 24.Rxe4 Qa5 25.Nc3 Qf5 26.f3 h5, and after 27.Kg1 the engine had you at +0.3. Everything was fine.

27...Rd8?? was the blunder, dropping to -5.1; 27...Kg7 was safe. 28.Re8+ Rxe8 cleared the diagonal for White's queen, and 29.Qxf5 took your queen for a rook. 29...g4 30.hxg4 Re1+ was only a last try before you resigned after 31.Kf2.

review.turning_point: 27...Rd8?? left your queen on f5 exposed, and 28.Re8+ cleared the path for 29.Qxf5.
review.focus: Before 27...Rd8, check White's checks. 27...Kg7 kept the king safe and your queen covered; always look for a check that also opens a line to your queen.

review.headline: A wild Bird Opening melee that you won with a late queen fork

sections.text: In this Bird Opening you got a comfortable position with 3...h6 and 5...e6, and after 9...e5 10.fxe5 Nxe5 11.e4 Bg4 you were fine. 12.h3 Bh5? is a good moment to notice: your bishop put a pin on the knight on f3 against the queen on d1.

13.g4 Nfxg4? was the first real mistake; 13...dxe4 was better. White answered with 14.Nxe5??, a discovered attack that unveiled the queen on g4, but you found 14...Bxe5!, the best move. 15.Rb1? then helped you, though 15...Ne3?? forked queen and rook, only for 16.Qxh5 to take your bishop; 15...Bd4+ was needed.
17...Nxd2? and later 23...Rf8? made things harder. White was ahead by 22.Bxh6, and 23.Rf1?? only partly saved you; 23...Kh7 was the right way to defend.
The turnaround was 27.Bh6??. You found 27...Qg6+!, a fork of the king on g2 and the bishop on h6. After 29.h4 Rxe6 you were back in the game. 30...Re2+? let White off, and 33.Qxa6?? Qxa6! ended it.

review.turning_point: 27.Bh6?? allowed 27...Qg6+!, which forked the king and the bishop and swung the game by almost eight pawns.
review.focus: Look at 15...Ne3. It looked strong, but 15...Bd4+ kept the advantage. Before playing a flashy knight move, check which of your own pieces is left hanging.

review.headline: A greedy bishop capture and a queen move that lost material at once

sections.text: You met the Polish with 1...e5 and took the pawn with 2...Bxb4. White's 3.Bxe5 returned the pawn with a strong bishop on the long diagonal aimed at g7 and the rook on h8.
3...Qe7?? was the blunder, dropping you from +0.2 to -4.3. 3...Nf6 was the move, covering g7 and developing. After 4.Bxg7 you were a pawn down, and 4...Nf6 5.Bxh8 took your rook.
The rest was a fight to complicate. 5...Ne4 6.Bc3 Nxf2?! was a fork of the queen on d1 and the rook on h1, but 7.Kxf2 simply took the knight, and the engine had you at -5.8.
7...Qh4+ 8.g3 Bc5+ 9.e3 Qe4 produced checks but nothing concrete. After 10.Nf3 d5 11.Bd3, you resigned. Early on, always ask which of your pieces the long diagonal is attacking.

review.turning_point: 3...Qe7?? ignored the bishop's diagonal, and 4.Bxg7 followed by 5.Bxh8 cost you both a pawn and the rook.
review.focus: At 3...Qe7 you needed to count what the bishop on e5 hit. 3...Nf6 covered g7 and developed at the same time.

review.headline: A dominant opening thrown away by sharp, unsafe middlegame choices

sections.text: In this Italian you obtained a great position. After 5.d4 exd4 6.cxd4 Bb4+ 7.Nc3 Nf6, 8.a3? was a small slip (8.e5 was the idea). Black's 8...Ba5?? put a pin on your knight on c3, but you found 9.b4!, the best move, which hit the bishop at once.
10.e5?! was slightly loose. Black's 10...Qe7?? pinned the e5 pawn against your king on e1, but it left you at +5.5 and the engine's best move was 10...d5. At that moment you simply needed to castle.

11.Qe2?? broke the evaluation from +5.5 to -0.7; 11.O-O was clearly stronger. After 11...Ng4?? you could still have fought, but 12.Ng5?? (12.Nd5 was better) and 12...d5?? 13.Bxd5?? lost the thread. 13.Nxd5 was the move.
After 13...Nxd4 14.Bxf7+?! Kf8 15.Qe4?! Bf5 16.Qxb7 Qxe5+ your king was exposed. 17.Be3 Nc2+ 18.Kf1?! Ngxe3+ 19.fxe3 Nxe3+ 20.Ke1 Nxg2+ 21.Kd2 Rd8+ 22.Kc1 Qxc3# was a perfect mating pattern.

review.turning_point: 11.Qe2?? turned +5.5 into -0.7, when castling with 11.O-O kept your advantage.
review.focus: At 11.Qe2 you left your king in the centre with the queen on e7 aiming at e1. When ahead, castle first: 11.O-O would have kept all your pieces safe.

review.headline: A messy Owen Defense where you survived, then hit back hard

sections.text: Against the Owen you set up with 4.Bd3, 5.O-O, 6.b3 and 7.Bb2, a sensible plan. Black's 10...c5? gave you a chance, but 11.d5? went for the wrong idea: 11.dxc5 Bxb2 was better. After 14.fxe5?! fxe5 the position was still level.
17.Bxe5?? was the real blunder; 17.Nxe5 was the move. After 17...dxe5 18.Nxe5 you were down material and about -3 in the engine's eyes.

Black helped with 19...Qf4?, since 19...Ng4 was better, but 20.Nd4?? gave the advantage back. After 20...Qe3+ 21.Qf2?! Qxd3?? you took chances again. 22.Ne6! was the best move, hitting the bishop on g7.

Black's 22...Nf5?? allowed 23.exf5!, and 23...Ng4?? was another slip. 24.Nxg7+! Kd7 25.Qf3 forked Black's queen and knight. 27.Qxf5+! and 29.Nxd4 won the queen, and after 35.Nc3 Black ran out of time.

review.turning_point: 22.Ne6! punished Black's grab on d3 and changed a lost position into a winning attack.
review.focus: Look at 17.Bxe5. A simple 17.Nxe5 kept the balance. Before giving up a bishop for a pawn, count what the recapture opens.

review.headline: A topsy-turvy QGD where you out-tricked White at the end

sections.text: A Queen's Gambit Declined with 4...Bb4+ and 8...Bxc3 9.bxc3 gave you doubled pawns to aim at. 9...e5?! was a bit hasty, and after 10.cxd5 Nxd5 11.c4 Nf6 12.dxe5 you were behind in the engine's eyes.
12...Nxe5?? was a blunder (12...Nd7 was better). After 13.Nxe5 Rxe5, White had a clear edge. But 14.Bb2?? missed 14.Bxh7+, and 14...Re6?? gave the edge back; 14...Re8 was the move.

15.Bf5?? was another White slip, and 15...Rd6! was exactly right: the rook leaving e6 was a discovered attack from your bishop on c8 to the bishop on f5. 16.Qc2 Rd2?! then hit the queen and bishop along the second rank.
After 17.Rfd1 Rxd1+ 18.Rxd1 Qe7 19.Bxf6 Qxf6?! 20.Bxh7+ Kh8 21.Be4 Be6 22.Bxb7 Rb8, you were slightly worse, but 23.Bd5?? Rb2! and 24.Qa4?? Qxf2+! 25.Kh1 Bxd5 turned the game around.

review.turning_point: 23.Bd5?? allowed 23...Rb2!, and after 24.Qa4?? your 24...Qxf2+! decided the game.
review.focus: Look at 12...Nxe5 and 14...Re6. Both let White's bishop tactics in. In middlegames with opposite pieces on the b2-h8 diagonal, check Bxh7+ before moving a rook.

review.headline: A short Italian win after Black walked into a pawn grab and a knight loss

sections.text: You played the Bc4 line against 3...Be7, with 4.d4 exd4 5.Nxd4 Nxd4 6.Qxd4 Bf6 7.e5 Qe7, giving you an early lead in the centre. The engine had you at about +1.1.
8.O-O? was a mistake; 8.f4 d6 kept the attack going. Black's 8...Bg5?? returned the favour, jumping to +4.1 for you instead of taking 8...Bxe5.
9.e6?? gave back most of that advantage; 9.f4 Bh6 was the better way to keep it. After 9...dxe6 10.Qxg7 Bf6 11.Qg3 you were still fine.
Black's 11...Nh6?? ran into 12.Bxh6!, taking the knight, and Black resigned. Quick and sharp.

review.turning_point: 11...Nh6?? left the knight hanging to 12.Bxh6!, which ended the game.
review.focus: Look at 9.e6. When opponents blunder, keep your structure with 9.f4 instead of sacrificing a pawn.

review.headline: A turbulent Pirc where the tactics finally went your way

sections.text: In the Pirc, 5.e5?! dxe5 6.Nxe5 O-O 7.Bc4 c5 8.Be3 Bf5 gave Black a good game. 9.d5? Qb6 10.Bb3 Qc7 kept the position balanced, but 11.Bf4?? was a blunder: 11.Nc4 was the move.

Black returned the favour with 11...Qb6??, and after 12.Nc4 Qa6 13.Bxb8 Raxb8 you traded your bishop for a knight. 14.g4?? was another risky pawn push, and 15.Ne5 c4? let you play 16.Bxc4!, picking up a pawn.
17.g5?? and 18.f3?? were questionable, since 18.Nxg4 was needed. 18...Bxf3 forked queen and rook, but 19.Qxf3! simply took the bishop and put you ahead.

20.Nd7?? forked queen and both rooks, but Black could have played 20...Qxb2. After 20...Rbd8?? you took the queen with 21.Nxb6!, and the rest was technique: 24.d6, 31.Bxf7+ and 38.Qxe8+. Black ran out of time on move 42.

review.turning_point: 20...Rbd8?? ignored the threat to the queen, and 21.Nxb6! won it.
review.focus: Look at 17.g5. Advancing pawns in front of your own king invited counterplay; 17.Bb3 kept things safe.

review.headline: An ambitious bishop sacrifice that did not work

sections.text: You played the Sicilian Taimanov with 4.Nxd4 Nc6 5.Nxc6 bxc6 6.Nc3 Qc7. 7.g3?! and 10.Bg5?! drifted from the best plan, and by 12.O-O the engine had you at about -0.9.

15.Bxh6?? was the decisive error. The engine preferred 15.Bf4 Bd6, which would have skewered the queen on c7 against the rook on b8 before it moved away. After 15...gxh6 16.Qxh6 Nh7 you did not have enough for the piece.
17.Ne4?! dxe4 18.Bxe4 f5 19.Qg6+ Kh8 20.Bd3 Rf6 21.Qe8+ Rf8 22.Qg6 Bf6 added more pieces but not enough threats. Black stayed calm and the evaluation reached -5.
24.Qh5 Rxb2 and then 25.f3?, which allowed a forced mate. 25...Rxb1 26.Rxb1 Qxg3+ 27.Kf1 followed, and you resigned.

review.turning_point: 15.Bxh6?? gave up a bishop for a pawn without a follow-up.
review.focus: At 15.Bxh6 check whether the sacrifice has a second wave. If not, 15.Bf4 keeps the bishop active.

review.headline: A solid defence that turned on one slip in the bishop ending

sections.text: The Colle went quietly: 4.Bb5+ Bd7 5.Bd3 Nc6 6.b3 Bd6?! 7.Ba3 a6 8.Bxd6 cxd6. After 9.Nbd2 e5 10.dxe5 dxe5 11.Be2 e4 12.Nd4 Nxd4 13.exd4 the position was balanced.

14.h3? gave you a chance, but 14...Re8?! 15.Nf1 Rc8?! 16.Ne3 Qe7?! were slightly passive. 19...Qb4+? missed 19...dxc4, but White answered with 22.Bxc4?, where 22.bxc4 was stronger, and you were equal again.
Trades followed: 25.Rxc7 Rxc7 26.Rc1 Rxc1 27.Kxc1 Nd5 28.Nxd5 Bxd5. You reached a bishop endgame at 0.0 and held it for many moves.

35...g6?? was the blunder; 35...f4+ was the move. After 36.fxe4+ fxe4 37.Bd1 Ke6?! 38.Bc2 Kd5?, 39.Bxe4+ took the pawn. Then 44.d5+ and 47.d6+ gave White the passed pawn, and you resigned after 65 moves.

review.turning_point: 35...g6?? let White open the f-file and win the e4 pawn.
review.focus: At 35...g6 you needed to calculate the pawn break. 35...f4+ kept the balance. In pawn endings, count each tempo.

review.headline: A big attack that slipped to a draw

sections.text: In the Scandinavian, 3.Nc3?! gave Black comfortable development, but 8...e6? let you play 9.O-O!, the best move. 10.a4? was a small slip; 10.h3 was cleaner. Still, 11.b4 and 12.a5 gave you space on the queenside.

13.c4?? was a blunder. After 13...Qd6? 14.b5?! axb5?? 15.cxb5?? the position got messy; 15.a6 was stronger. 16.a6 Bxf3? 17.Bxf3! was the correct recapture, and 18.Qxf3 g4 19.Qxb7+ Kd7 pushed Black's king into the open.

20.Bg5?? pinned the bishop on e7 against the rook on d8, but Black could just take with 20...Bxg5. Instead 20...Ke8?? allowed 21.Bxe7?!, which forked the queen and the rook. Then 23.a8=Q?? gave up the advantage, since 23.Qxb6 was better.
After 27...g3?? 28.hxg3! e5 29.R7a5 e4?? 30.Re5+! you were clearly better at +3.3, but with 36.Kh2?! and 40.Rhf4, the rooks shuffled between h4 and f4 and the game ended as a draw.

review.turning_point: 23.a8=Q?? cost your advantage; 23.Qxb6 kept it.
review.focus: At 23.a8=Q you promoted without checking the consequences. 23.Qxb6 was the strongest move; always check for the simple capture before promoting.

review.headline: A refuted gambit and a big edge, then time pressure turned a winning endgame into a draw

sections.text: You met the Cochrane Gambit well. 4.Nxf7 forks your queen and rook, but 4...Kxf7! is the best reply and leaves you ahead. 5...Ke8? gave back some of the edge (the engine preferred 5...d5), yet after 6.d4 Nxe4 you were a clear pawn up and the evaluation stayed above +2 for the next thirty moves.

You then played the sensible plan of trading down: 17.Qxf6+ Bxf6 took the queens off, 18.Rxe8 Kxe8 traded rooks, and 23...Bxc1 removed a bishop. When your opponent tried 29.c4+?, you took it with 29...Kxc4! and the evaluation climbed toward +4.5.

Then the clock got you. 36...Rxf3?? dropped the evaluation from +4.3 to +0.3; 36...Nxf3+ was a discovered attack that kept everything protected. Your opponent returned the favour with 37.Rd1+??, and you found 37...Rd3!, but 38...Rf3?? repeated the mistake and 39.Rd1+?? repeated theirs.

40...Kd2?? was the last slip: 40.Re1+ is a skewer along the e-file, and after 41.Rxe5 you were suddenly worse at -2.9. You defended well afterwards, and 43...Kd3! kept the rook ending balanced until the draw.

review.turning_point: 36...Rxf3?? in time trouble, which swung +4.3 to +0.3 and set off the chain of mistakes that ended with 40...Kd2??.
review.focus: When you are ahead and short on time, take the safest forcing move. At 36...Rxf3 the move 36...Nxf3+ kept all your pieces protected, so check what a capture leaves undefended before playing it.

review.headline: A clean Italian where one queen swap left you a piece up

sections.text: You played the Italian with the usual c3 and d4 plan, and 4...h6 from your opponent was slow enough that you were already at +1.2. After 5.d4 Bb6 you took the pawn with 6.Nxe5 Nxe5 7.dxe5, a knight swap that left you a pawn up with a strong pawn on e5.

7...Qh4 went after the e4 pawn and f2, and 8.Qf3 guarded both while keeping your development moving. Then 8...Nf6? kicked your e5 pawn (the engine preferred 8...Qe7), and you found the right answer, 9.exf6!, simply taking the knight. After 9...Qxf6 10.Qxf6 gxf6 the queens were off and you were a clean piece ahead.

From there it was good technique. 11.O-O and 12.Bf4 finished development, 13.exd5 cxd5 14.Re1+ Kf8 kept Black's king stuck in the middle, and 15.Bxd5 collected another pawn. 16.Re7 put a rook on the seventh rank, and 17.Nd2 and 18.Rae1 brought in the rest of your army.
19.Bxe6 fxe6 20.R1xe6 ended the game with you five points of material up, and your opponent resigned.

review.turning_point: 9.exf6! After 8...Nf6? you took the knight and let the queens come off, which turned a good position into a piece-up endgame.
review.focus: There were no errors to fix, so the habit to keep is what you did at 9.exf6: at every opponent mistake, look at the capture first. Next time, also compare your plan with the engine's quieter idea after 9.exf6 d5 of 10.Be2.

review.headline: A wild pawn-storm game where a missed capture nearly cost you, until a knight check settled it

sections.text: Both sides came out swinging. 2...f6 and 3...g5? loosened your own king; the engine suggested 3...Nh6, and by 4.Bg3 the evaluation had slipped to -0.8. You kept going with 4...h5 and 5...h4, and after 7...e5 8.dxe5 fxe5 you had a healthy centre and the more active pieces.

Your opponent then helped. 11.Bg6? was a mistake, and after 12.Bd3 Nf6 13.Nc3 Be6 you were around +1. The big chance came with 17.Nxd5+??, which put you at +3.8. Capturing with 17...Bxd5 was the move; 17...Kd8?? threw it away and the evaluation went to -2.0.

More slips followed. 21...Nb4?? was another one (the engine wanted 21...Be6), and the evaluation stayed around -2 to -3. But you kept finding active moves, and 22...Nxh2 23.Rxh2 Rxh2 24.Nxh2 traded down while your opponent's king stayed awkward.
The end came when they played 26.Qg3??, missing 26.O-O-O. Your 26...Nxc2+! is a fork of the king and the rook on a1, and 27.Kd2 Nxa1 left you well ahead in material, so your opponent resigned.

review.turning_point: 17...Kd8?? after 17.Nxd5+??: 17...Bxd5 was available and winning, and instead the evaluation went from +3.8 to -2.0. The game was later saved by 26...Nxc2+!.
review.focus: When the opponent drops a piece, look at the capture before the king move. At 17...Kd8 you had 17...Bxd5; ask yourself every time what the simplest recapture does for your position.

review.headline: A pure punish-the-blunder win: one queen move took a knight and the game was decided

sections.text: You met 3...h6 in the Italian with 4.d4, and after 4...Nf6 5.dxe5 the position was fine for you. Then your opponent played 5...Nxe4??, grabbing a pawn that cost a piece.
6.Qd5! was the right answer. It attacks the loose knight on e4 and keeps f7 under pressure with the bishop behind, and 6...Qe7 7.Qxe4 simply won the knight. From +1.3 the evaluation jumped to +5.

After that you did everything right: 8.O-O developed, 8...Nxe5 9.Nxe5 dxe5 simplified, and 10.Re1 and 11.Qg6+ Kd8 12.Rd1+ Bd7 kept Black's king in the middle. 13.Nc3, 14.Be3 and 15.Ne4 brought your other pieces in, and 20.Be6 Kb8 21.Rxd7 Rxd7 22.Qxd7 cleaned up.

23.b4?! was the only inaccuracy. It does hit the queen and bishop, but 23...Bxb4 just takes it, and 23.Qxg7 was cleaner. You were so far ahead that it did not matter, and 24.Qxg7 Rd8 25.Rb1 Bxa3 26.Qxb7# finished it.

review.turning_point: 6.Qd5! right after 5...Nxe4??: you found the move that won the knight back with interest.
review.focus: At 23.b4 you went for a flashy move when 23.Qxg7 kept the attack going with no concessions. In winning positions, check whether your pawn can simply be taken before playing it.

review.headline: A comfortable Petrov that you pushed too far on the kingside until the king ran out of cover

sections.text: You played the Petrov accurately. 3...d6 and 4...Nxe4 gave you a normal game, 9...Nxc3 doubled White's pawns with 10.bxc3, and when White tried 14.Ne5? you found 14...Nxe5!, which kept the evaluation in your favour.

The trouble started with the pawn advance on the kingside. 17...f5 was fine, but 18...f4? (the engine preferred 18...b5) pushed the pawn past the point of safety and opened lines against your own king. 19.c4 Be4 20.Qg4 kept the pressure on.
20...f3?? was the big error. It left you facing 21.Qxg7#, which your opponent missed with 21.g3??. That gave you a second chance, and 21...Bf6! was a good defensive move.
Then came 22...cxd5??, which turned a manageable position into -5.2. The engine's 22...Bxd5 kept things together. After 23.Bxf6 Rxf6 24.Qxe4 the bishop on e4 was lost and you resigned.

review.turning_point: 20...f3?? walked into a forced mate that White missed, and then 22...cxd5?? gave back the rescue.
review.focus: Before pushing a pawn near your own king, count what it opens. At 20...f3 the engine's 20...Bf6 kept you alive; ask what White's queen on g4 does once the f-pawn passes.

review.headline: A Sicilian that took one wrong queen swap to throw away a big advantage, then won anyway

sections.text: A normal open Sicilian: 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nc6 5.Bc4 Nf6 6.Nxc6 bxc6 7.Nc3 g6. 8.e5 attacked the knight, and your opponent answered with 8...dxe5??, a discovered attack that exposed their own queen on the d-file and put you at +4.9.
You then played 9.Qxd8+??, which cost almost all of it. The engine's 9.Bxf7+ Kxf7 10.Qxd8 kept your edge. After 9...Kxd8 you were a pawn down and the evaluation was +0.2.
10.Bg5 was a good developing move, and your opponent returned the favour with 10...Be6??. It allowed 11.O-O-O+ Ke8 12.Bxe6 fxe6, which gave you a lead in development again at +2.1.
14...Nxh2 looked greedy, but 15.Rh1 Nxf3 16.gxf3 won the knight back and you were comfortably ahead. 17.Ne4 and 18.Rd7 finished the job and your opponent resigned.

review.turning_point: 9.Qxd8+??, where the capture that looks natural gave away +4.9 and the engine's 9.Bxf7+ kept it.
review.focus: After 8...dxe5 your opponent had hung the position; slow down at moments like 9.Qxd8+ and ask whether a check first (9.Bxf7+) wins more than the obvious queen capture.

review.headline: A London System you out-played with a bishop trade and a cool middlegame, then crushed with a rook grab

sections.text: You met the London well. 3...Bd6 and 4...Bxf4 traded off White's best bishop, and 5.exf4 left them with a weaker pawn structure. 6...b6 and 7...Bb7 aimed your bishop down the long diagonal, and 10...Nxc5?! and 11...d4 kept the centre open.

The only real slip from you was 12...O-O?, which let the evaluation turn to -0.7. The engine suggested 12...d3 first. You recovered with 13...Qd5 and 14...Qh5?!, a discovered attack that unveiled your bishop on b7 against f3 and also pinned the knight to the queen on e2.
White lost the thread with 15.b4??. After 15...Nb3 your knight attacked the rook on a1, and 16.Rd1 Nxd4 17.Rxd4 Bxf3 18.Qe3 Bxh1 picked up a knight and then the rook on h1. Material read +7 for you.
The rest was simple. 26...Qxe1+ 27.Kxe1 Rxe6+ traded queens and left you with a rook and bishop attack, and the rooks finished the game. Your opponent resigned after 33...Bc6.

review.turning_point: 15.b4?? by White, which let 15...Nb3 hit the rook and brought the evaluation from -1.4 to +3.7.
review.focus: The one mistake was 12...O-O?: castling moved the king before dealing with the d-pawn. Look at 12...d3 next time before you tuck your king away.

review.headline: A Bird Opening won by an early exchange gain and a tactical finish

sections.text: You answered 1.f4 with 1...d5 and a solid setup. 6...d4?! gave you space in the centre, and 7.e4 Bb4+?! 8.Bd2 O-O?! 9.Bxb4 Nxb4 got your pieces out. Some of the moves were inaccuracies, but White was not punishing them.
The turning point was 13.c4??. After 12.e5 Nd5 it let your knight jump to e3. 13...Ne3 14.Qd2 Nxf1 won the exchange, and the evaluation rose to +1.7.
You played the middlegame sensibly: 15...b6, 16...Bb7, then 21.Nbd2 axb5 and 25.Nb3 Rxa4 26.Rxa4 Bxa4 opened lines for your bishop. After 27.Nbxd4 you were around +4.

Then two of your own errors cost some of it. 28...b5? (the engine wanted 28...Nc3) and 29...Rb8? (29...Nxf4 was better) let White back in. But 31.Nxa4? was a mistake from them, and 31...Qxd4+! is a fork of the king on g1 and the knight on a4. You came out well ahead and your opponent resigned.

review.turning_point: 13.c4?? by White: it allowed 13...Ne3, which won the exchange and set up everything that followed.
review.focus: 28...b5? and 29...Rb8? let a +5.5 position drift toward +2.8. Look at 29...Nxf4 and 28...Nc3: when you are winning, use your knight actively instead of making a pawn move.

review.headline: A quick Accelerated Dragon where the opponent ignored a hit on their queen

sections.text: You met the Accelerated Dragon with the standard plan: 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5.Bc4 Bg7 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Nc3 O-O 8.O-O. It was balanced, and the evaluation hovered around zero for the whole opening.

Black grabbed the pawn with 8...Nxe4, but 9.Nxe4 d5 attacked your knight and the position stayed level after 10.Bxd5 Qxd5. Black's queen now stood on d5, in the middle of your pieces, and that became the target.

11.Nc3 hit the queen straight away, and Black chose the one reply that does not deal with it. After 11...Nxd4?? the queen was still en prise, and you found 12.Nxd5!, which won the queen and moved the evaluation from -0.5 to +5.3. They resigned.

review.turning_point: 11...Nxd4?? by Black. 12.Nxd5! punished it at once by taking the queen.
review.focus: Accuracy was high, but 8.O-O allowed 8...Nxe4 with a threat of its own. Before castling in an open Sicilian, check whether the e4 pawn is loose after 8.O-O.

review.headline: A Scandinavian where one natural-looking knight move lost a piece and the queen finished the job

sections.text: You played the Scandinavian by the book: 2.exd5 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nxd5 4.d4 Bg4 5.Be2 e6 6.h3 Bh5. 7.c4 gained a tempo on the knight on d5, and the evaluation was a comfortable +0.6.

Black replied 7...Nf4??, which just loses a piece; the engine's 7...Nb6 was the right retreat. You found 8.Bxf4!, a pin on the c7 pawn against the knight on b8, and after 8...Bd6 9.Bxd6 cxd6 you were up a clean piece at +5.7.
10.Qa4+ Ke7 11.Qb5 attacked the loose bishop on h5 and the pawn on b7 at the same time. Black could not hold both, and 11...b6 12.Qxh5 picked up the bishop, so you were far ahead.
13.Qg5+ f6 14.Qxg7+ Ke8 15.Qxh8+ finished the game with the queen taking pawns and a rook while the black king had nowhere to hide. It was a very clean, fast conversion.

review.turning_point: 7...Nf4?? by Black. 8.Bxf4! was the only move needed, and it won a piece outright.
review.focus: A very accurate game. For improvement, review the line after 7.c4 where Black plays 7...Nb6 and see how you would proceed, so the plan is ready if the opponent does not blunder.

review.headline: A double-edged Sicilian where you outplayed your opponent tactically and then lost a winning race

sections.text: 9.Nxe5?! was ambitious. Black answered with 9...Nxd3+??, a fork of the bishop on b2 and the king, but you then played 10.cxd3?? (10.Nxd3 was the engine move). Luckily 10...Ne7?? was a worse error and you steadied with 11.Nf3!, which kept the balance.

You built up well with 12.O-O and 14.Rc1, though 15.e5? and 16.Qf4?! cost you some of the edge. Then Black's 18...f4?? allowed 19.Nxe6!, and 22.Rxc5! was a very good follow-up. You emerged clearly ahead in material.
Your play then became less precise. 24.Ke1?!, 26.Ne4?! and 28.Kc3?! let the evaluation fall, and 33.b4? was a mistake that took it near +1.

The critical moment was 34.Rxc5+?, which looks like a fork of the king and rook but allowed 34...Kxd6. 35.Rxe5?? then left Black's d-pawn free to run, and after 36.Ka4 d5 the pawn could not be stopped. You lost with the black queen delivering 53...Qxb7#.

review.turning_point: 34.Rxc5+? and 35.Rxe5??: you traded into a pawn race where your king was too far away from the d-pawn.
review.focus: In an endgame that you still control, take the simple route. At 34.Rxc5+ the engine's 34.bxc5 kept your advantage; before trading rooks, count the pawn race.

review.headline: A chaotic Italian that you won on tactics, even though you were the one who blundered first

sections.text: The opening looked normal until 7.O-O?! Nxe4 8.Re1?!, which pinned the knight on e4 against the king. After 8...d5 you had the chance to take the pawn with 9.Bxd5, but 9.Nfd2?? let the evaluation drop to -2.4.

Your opponent returned the favour with 9...Qh4?? and 10...Qe7??, which put you back in a good position, but 10.g3?? and 11.f3?? were bad weakening moves. 11.f3?? took you from +3.9 to -5.5, and after 12.Bxd5?? Bxd4+ you were in real trouble.

You found a good defence with 14.hxg3! after 13...Nxg3+??, and Black's 14...Qf6?? gave it all back. 16.Bxc6?? allowed a forced mate, but 16...bxc6?? missed it. 17.Qxd4! and 20.Qxd8! showed good tactical vision.
27.Nd5?? allowed a forced mate again and 27...hxg3?? missed it. After 31.Nf6+! and 32.exf6 gxf6 you were winning cleanly, and 42.a8=Q and 43.Qh8# finished the game.

review.turning_point: 14.hxg3! and 17.Qxd4!, where you picked up material after Black's blunders and took over the game.
review.focus: Your king safety needs work. 10.g3 and 11.f3 left your king exposed, so before pushing f- and g-pawns near your own king, check the diagonals. 11.f3 is the move to study.

review.headline: A Queen's Gambit Declined that you won on time after throwing away a big edge

sections.text: You played the QGD solidly. 7.c5 b6 8.cxb6 axb6 liquidated the queenside, and after 11.Bxa5 Bxb5 12.Bxb5 Rxa5 the pieces had traded evenly. 14...Qd6 and 15...g5 gave you an active, if risky, setup.

16...c6? was a small mistake (the engine wanted 16...c5), and 20...Rb5?? was a bigger one: 20...Qb5 was the better move. Your opponent then played 23.Nxb5??, a discovered attack that opened the d-file on your queen. The right reply was 23...Qxa2, which took the queen and left you at +4.3.
You played 23...Qxb5?? instead, and the evaluation flipped from +4.3 to -3.8. From there the engine rated you at -3 to -6 for the rest of the game.
32...Qxc1+? grabbed a rook with check, but 33.Qxc1 simply recaptured, and the engine preferred 32...Qd3. You kept playing, your opponent ran out of time on move 37, and you took the win on the clock.

review.turning_point: 23...Qxb5??, which let a +4.3 position turn into -3.8 when 23...Qxa2 was available.
review.focus: When your opponent's capture opens a line, check what is now attacked before you recapture. At 23...Qxb5 the move 23...Qxa2 would have won the game.

review.headline: A Petrov with a great middlegame attack that fell apart in time trouble

sections.text: A Three Knights Petrov where 4...Be6 invited 5.Bxe6 fxe6, which gave you a half-open f-file. 8.Qd2? and 10.Kb1?? from White let you strike with 10...d4!, a pawn fork of the knight on c3 and the bishop on e3.
You then ran White off the board. 11...dxc3 12.Qxc3, 14...O-O-O and 17...hxg4 built pressure, 18...exf4! took more, and 21...Rxh2 22.Qd4 Rxf2 23.Qxf2 left you well ahead.
29...Nce3?? was the first real error; it is a fork on the rook and queen, but 30.Nxe3 Nxe3 31.Qxf2 left things close to level. The engine's 29...Qb6 kept the advantage.

You were also low on time. 38...c5?, 40...Rxd3??, 42...Kc6?? and 45...Ka5?? gave away good positions; 40...cxd3 was the move at the critical moment. The game ended with your flag falling after 46.Rc5+.

review.turning_point: 40...Rxd3??, where a winning position turned into a forced loss when 40...cxd3 was available.
review.focus: Time management is the issue: after 29...Nce3?? you were burning clock while the position was still winning. Practice picking safe moves quickly, and use 40...cxd3 as an example.

review.headline: A Petrov blunder on move three, saved by a calm defence and a big swing at move 29

sections.text: 3...Nxe4?? lost a piece in the Three Knights Petrov (the engine preferred 3...Nc6). After 4.Nxe4 d5 5.Ng3 e4 the evaluation sat around -3, and White kept a clear edge for nearly thirty moves.

You fought back. 8...Bxf5 traded off a strong knight, and 16...Qxa4 pinned the knight on a3 to the rook on a1. 18.dxe4 fxe4 and 22.Qxe4+ Qxe4+ 23.Bxe4 Bxa1 brought you chances, and 21...d3 kept the pawn on the board.
Then White blundered with 29.Bb2+?? and you found 29...Bxb2! (the engine move was 29.Bxc6). The evaluation went from -5.7 to +3.6, and 30.Nxb2 Nd4 started a decisive attack with the pawn on c2.
You promoted with 32...c1=Q and continued with 36...Rxg4. 41...a2 followed by 42...a1=Q gave you another queen, and 47...Qxf2# finished the game.

review.turning_point: 29.Bb2+?? and your reply 29...Bxb2!, where the evaluation turned from -5.7 to +3.6.
review.focus: The problem was 3...Nxe4: in the Three Knights it only works if you have a follow-up. 3...Nc6 was safe, so learn the main plan against 3.Nc3 before grabbing the pawn.

review.headline: An Italian where two pawn pushes opened your position and the opponent took advantage

sections.text: A normal Italian: 4.c3 d6 5.d4 exd4 6.cxd4 Bb6. Then 7.e5? was a mistake that dropped the evaluation to -0.8; 7.Nc3 was the engine move. After 7...Bg4 your pieces were stretched.

8.d5?? made it worse, taking you to -2.3. 8...Nxe5 attacked your knight and bishop, and the engine suggested 8.h3 instead. 9.Qe2?! and 10.Qe4?! kept the queen active but 10...Bxf3 11.gxf3 wrecked your pawns.

12.a4 Nxc4 13.Qxc4 left you a pawn down with a damaged structure, and your opponent made a mistake with 13...Qh3??, which gave you a chance. But 14.Qg4?? let the queens come off and you were still worse.
After 16.O-O Nxd5 the position was bad, and 19...Re2 and 20...Rxf2 kept the pressure on. You resigned after 21.Kh1 Ne3.

review.turning_point: 8.d5??, which was the move that turned a slightly worse position into a losing one.
review.focus: After 7...Bg4 you need to count attackers before pushing pawns. 8.d5?? ignored 8...Nxe5, so check what a pawn move leaves unprotected.

review.headline: A Queen's Pawn game with plenty of errors on both sides that you won with a queen trade and passed pawns

sections.text: You set up a classical structure with 4...Bd6 and 5...O-O, and 6...e5 and 9...c5 broke in the centre. After 10.dxc5 bxc5 11.bxc5 Bxc5 the position was balanced, but 12...d4?? was an error (the engine wanted 12...Nbd7) and took you to -2.3.
14...Qb6? and 16...Qe7? made it worse. The engine suggested 14...Nbd7 and 16...Qc7. 17...h5? then left the evaluation near -2.8, though White's 17.a5?? had already given back a lot.
Then White blundered with 18.Nxh5??, and you found 18...Qxe2!, taking the bishop. After 19.Nxf6+ gxf6 20.Qxe2 Rxe2 the queens were off and the evaluation swung to +1.8.
You converted well: 22...Nxa5, then the a-pawn ran with 27...a4, 32...a3 and 33...a2. 31...Nxc1 won the exchange and White resigned after 37...Rb1+.

review.turning_point: 18.Nxh5?? by White, which let 18...Qxe2! turn a -2.8 position into +1.6.
review.focus: You made four errors in the middlegame, starting with 12...d4??. Look at 12...Nbd7 and ask what it kept: tension in the centre without leaving the bishop on c5 loose.

review.headline: A Sicilian where early chances slipped and a kingside pawn storm backfired

sections.text: A normal Sicilian into 6.Bg5 and 8.O-O-O. After 9.Bd3 your opponent played 9...b5??, which gave you +2.2, but 10.Kb1?? missed 10.Bxf6 and gave the advantage right back.
11.Qe2?! and 12.Be3? kept drifting; 12.Nxc6 was the engine move. After 13.f3 Rfc8 14.h4 Ne5 the pawn storm began, but 15.h5 h6 16.g4 Nc4 left your pieces stretched and your own king exposed.
17.g5? was a mistake (the engine preferred 17.Bxc4) and 18.Bxg5?? followed. 18...Nxb2 19.Kxb2 Qxc3+ 20.Kb1 Qxd4 was a disaster, and you were down material.
After 21.h6?! g6 22.h7+ Kh8 23.e5? Qxe5 you were well behind, and 28.Bxg6? made it worse in time trouble. You resigned after 29.Qg3 Bf6+.

review.turning_point: 10.Kb1?? and then 18.Bxg5??, where you missed the strong captures 10.Bxf6 and 18.Bxc4.
review.focus: Look for captures that remove the opponent's active pieces. At 17.g5 the engine's 17.Bxc4 would have removed the knight that later broke up your position.

review.headline: A Philidor where an early structural concession slowly cost you

sections.text: You went into a Philidor-style setup. 3...Be6 4.Bxe6 fxe6 gave you the half-open f-file but doubled pawns. 5.d4 exd4 6.Nxd4 e5?! kicked the knight, but it also let White choose where to put it.

White's 7.Nf5? was a mistake (the engine move was 7.Ne6), and you handled it well with 7...Ne7. After 8.Nxe7 Bxe7 9.O-O Nd7 the position was balanced and your play stayed accurate through 10.Qh5+ g6 11.Qh6 Bf8 12.Qe3 Bg7.
15...d5? was the one mistake. The evaluation went from -0.3 to -1.8, and the engine preferred 15...Nf6. After 16.exd5 cxd5 17.Nxd5 you were a pawn down and facing a strong knight on d5.
18...Nf6?! then let 19.Nxf6+ come with check, and you resigned. It was a short game with only one major error.

review.turning_point: 15...d5?, which opened the centre when White's pieces were better placed.
review.focus: Before opening the centre, check your piece placement. At 15...d5 the engine's 15...Nf6 kept the position closed, since White's pieces were better prepared than yours.

review.headline: A Nimzowitsch Defense where you out-developed your opponent and finished with a queen sacrifice

sections.text: You met 1...Nc6 with 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5 Ne4 5.Nxe4 dxe4, and 6.c3 and 7.Bb5 gave you space. 9.fxe4?! was a small inaccuracy (9.Qe2 was the engine move), but your opponent replied with 9...a6??, which cost them.

10.Bc4 b5 11.Bb3 and 12.Nf3 e6 kept your pieces active. 13.h3 Bxf3 14.Qxf3 then 14...b4? gave you an even bigger edge. 15.Bd2?! was a little loose (15.Ba4 was better), but 16.O-O and 17.Bg5 brought you to +4.5.

18.exf6 Nxd4 19.f7+?! was a discovered attack, since the pawn uncovers the bishop on g5 against the queen on e7. The engine preferred 19.Ba4+, but you were still fine. 20.Bxe7+ Bxe7 left you far ahead.
22.f8=Q+?! was flashy (22.bxc3 was cleaner). 22...Rxf8 23.Qxf8+! was a skewer, and after 23...Bxf8 24.Rxf8+ Ke7 25.Rxa8 you were well ahead. Your opponent resigned after 27.Bxc2.

review.turning_point: 19.f7+ and 20.Bxe7+, where the bishop and pawn combination won the queen for a bishop.
review.focus: Your tactics were strong but 22.f8=Q+?! gave up evaluation for flash. Look at 22.bxc3, which kept +8.7 without needing a sacrifice.

review.headline: A winning Petrov middlegame thrown away in time trouble

sections.text: This Three Knights Petrov stayed level for a long time. You traded down with 9...Nxe5 and 11...Bxe2 12.Qxe2 dxe5, and the engine had you at roughly equal. 16...c5?! and the quiet bishop moves 18...Bf8 and 19...Bg7 then gave you a small edge, which was fine.

White's 21.f4?? was the gift. You found 21...Rxd1!, and when White recaptured badly with 22.Rxd1? you replied 22...exf4!, which put you around +3.7. That was precise: you opened the long diagonal for your bishop and kept the extra material.
You kept pressing with 25...Qxd8 and 26...Qd1?!, and 28.e5 Bg5?! held a big edge at +3.5. The clock then started to hurt.

29.e6 fxe6?? was the first real slip: the engine wanted 29...Qd4+ 30.Kh1 Qf2. Worse came after 30.Qd7+, a fork of your king and queen. 30...Kh6?? allowed 31.Qxd1, when 30...Qxd7 was simply winning for you.

review.turning_point: 30.Qd7+ forked king and queen, and 30...Kh6?? lost the queen to 31.Qxd1 when 30...Qxd7 was available.
review.focus: On 30...Kh6 you were low on time and moved the king without looking at the queen. When a check hits your king, first ask whether you can capture the checking piece, as with 30...Qxd7.

review.headline: A clean Italian win where a trap on move 13 decided everything

sections.text: You went into an Italian against 3...h6 and played the sharp 4.d4 exd4 5.Nxd4 Nxd4 6.Qxd4, getting your queen to the centre early. 8.O-O?! and 9.e5 dxe5 10.Qxe5 were fine, but 11.Rd1?! and 12.Qb5? let Black equalise; the engine liked 12.Qd4.

Black then walked into it with 13...Be6??. You found 14.Bxe6! fxe6 15.Qxe6+ Kh8, winning a pawn and getting your queen into the open. 16.Bf4 Qd7 17.Qxd7 Nxd7 18.Bxd6 cxd6 19.Rxd6 left you two pawns up (+3.2).
20.Re1?! eased up, but 20...Ng4? let you play the careful 21.f3!. Then you traded pieces, doubled your rooks with 25.Ree7, and pushed the e-pawn with 33.e6, 35.e7 and 39.e8=Q.
The finish was tidy: 42.Qxg6+ Kxg6 left a rook ending with a-pawn ready, 49.a8=Q and 54.Qf1# ended it.

review.turning_point: 13...Be6?? allowed 14.Bxe6! fxe6 15.Qxe6+, which won a pawn and began a long winning edge.
review.focus: 12.Qb5? gave away the opening edge (-0.3 to -1.8). Your queen had a safe square at d4, so look for squares that keep the queen active and unattackable before you wander, as the engine's 12.Qd4 did.

review.headline: A wild French Gambit where both queens got blundered and you came out on top

sections.text: White went for a Diemer-Duhm style gambit and 3.c4? gave you a fine opportunity. You took it with 3...dxe4! and after 4.Nc3 Nf6 5.f3 Bb4 6.fxe4 Nxe4 you were up a pawn.

7.Bd2?? was a clear mistake for White. You took with 7...Nxd2?, which kept an advantage, but the engine preferred 7...Qxd4. After 8.Qxd2 Nc6?! 9.a3? you grabbed a pawn with 9...Qxd4??, which was the blunder: 9...Bxc3 was the right move.
White missed 10.axb4 and played 10.Qxd4??. Your reply 10...Nxd4! was excellent, and after 11.axb4 Nc2+ 12.Kd2 Nxa1 you were up material (+4).
13...Nb3? let some of the advantage go, but you cleaned up with 16...Nxe2 and 21...Bxd1, and later 24...Rexd3, and White resigned after 29.Kf4.

review.turning_point: 10.Qxd4?? gave White's queen away, and 10...Nxd4! with 12...Nxa1 won a decisive amount of material.
review.focus: 9...Qxd4?? took a pawn and left you with a loose bishop on b4. Before capturing in the opening, check that everything is defended; 9...Bxc3 was the engine's move.

review.headline: A short Scotch where one greedy pawn push opened your king

sections.text: You played the Scotch with 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 and then 5.Bg5?!, which pinned the knight but let Black respond comfortably with 5...Bc5. After 6.Nxc6 bxc6 the position was level.
7.e5? was the key mistake. It attacked the knight but allowed 7...Bxf2+, opening your king (-1.6). The engine's 7.Bd3 was calm and kept things level.
8.Kxf2?! (-2.4) took the bishop, but 8...Ne4+ gave Black a strong attack. Then 9.Ke1? left your bishop on g5 to be taken: 9...Qxg5, with 9.Kg1 better.
10.Qf3 Qc1+ 11.Ke2? ended the fight. The engine's 11.Qd1 was needed, and after 11...Ba6+ White resigned.

review.turning_point: 7.e5? allowed 7...Bxf2+ and began a series of checks that your king could not survive.
review.focus: 7.e5? was a pawn push that ignored your king. Before a pawn move in the opening, check whether it unprotects a square next to the king; 7.Bd3 was safe.

review.headline: A won game that slid away through blunders in time trouble

sections.text: You started with a solid e5/d6 setup and by 9.d5?? White had overextended. You replied 9...cxd5!, and after 10.exd5 Nxd5 11.Nxd5 Bxd5 you were a clear pawn up with a good position.

17...f4?? let some of that go (-0.2), but the real swing came with 18.Qxe4 Bf5?? and 19.Qd5+, a fork of your king and bishop. You answered 19...Kh8! and after 20.Qxf5 Bxc3 21.bxc3?? Rxf5! you had won a large amount of material (+4.8).
From there you were dominant (+5), and 28.Nxe5 dxe5 29.Rxe5 should have been easy. 29...Rxd3?? dropped to +0.4, though, and the game went into a rook endgame.

On the clock you played 44...Rf6?? (-7.1), recovered when White missed it with 45.Re8+, and then blundered again with 46...Re6??, 47...g5?? and 51...Kf5??. The last blow was 58...Kg8??, after which you lost on time.

review.turning_point: 29...Rxd3?? threw away a +4.9 position, and the later endgame errors were all made in time trouble.
review.focus: 58...Kg8?? lost a drawn pawn ending; 58...Kf8 59.Kg6 Kg8 held. In king and pawn endings, keep your king in front of the pawn and play the engine's 58...Kf8.

review.headline: A London where you won despite missing a mate in one

sections.text: Against the London you played 5...Ne4 and traded off the dangerous bishop with 6...Nxg3 7.hxg3. After 7...g6 you were slightly better, but 8...f6?? (engine 8...Nd7) and 9...e5?? loosened your own position.
White returned the favour. 9.Nbd2?? and 11.Nh4?? missed the strong Bxg6+ ideas, and after 12.Nxg6 exd3?? White's 13.Nxh8 and 14.Rxh7 won material. You were clearly worse for a while (-4.1).
Then 16.fxg3?? let you in. You found 16...Qxe3+!, and 17.Kf1 Be2+ 18.Ke1 should have ended with 18...Qxg3#. Instead 18...Qg1+?? dropped the evaluation to -0.1.
Both sides kept blundering, with 20...Qxa1?? and 21.Qxd5?? and 23.Kf4??. By 24.Qxd6 cxd6 25.Ng6 d2 your passed pawn won the game. You promoted with 27...d1=Q and finished with 52...Qh5#.

review.turning_point: 16.fxg3?? allowed 16...Qxe3+! and a forced mate that you missed with 18...Qg1+??, though you still won later.
review.focus: 18...Qg1+?? missed 18...Qxg3#. With the enemy king boxed in, check every queen capture that gives mate before playing a check.

review.headline: An Alapin where an early lead faded and a queen trade turned bad

sections.text: The Alapin with 2.Ne2?! and 3.g3?! was a slow start, and Black equalised without trouble. 9.Qc2?! Nfd7? let you gain a slight edge, and 11.d4 Bf6 12.dxe5 Nxe5 kept the position balanced.
13.O-O-O?? was the first blunder (+1.2 to -0.8); the engine liked 13.f4 Nc6. Black returned the favour with 14.Nf3?? Bc6??, and you found 15.Nxe5!, which brought you back to +2.0.
But 18.Bxe5?? (engine 18.f4) gave away your edge. After 20.fxe5 Rxe5? you were back in the game, then 21.Rhf1?! Qh6+ 22.Nf4?! Qxh2 let Black's queen run free.
23.Bh3? stepped off the g2 square and allowed 23...Qxc2+ 24.Kxc2, a queen trade into a worse ending (-2.2). 25.Nd5?! Nxe4 and 26.Rde1? left a piece to be won, and you resigned.

review.turning_point: 18.Bxe5?? threw away a +2.4 edge, and the evaluation never recovered.
review.focus: 13.O-O-O?? put your king on the queenside while Black's pieces already eyed it. Compare 13.f4 Nc6: it kept the king safe and the centre under control.

review.headline: A Scandinavian won by an intermezzo on move 12 and a rook mate

sections.text: You met the Scandinavian with 2.exd5 and 4.d4, and then developed calmly with 5.Nf3, 6.Be2 and 8.O-O, keeping a small edge. 9.Re1 Bb4 put Black's bishop on b4, which set up what came next.

10.Bd2? lost a little of that edge, and 10...Qxd4? grabbed a pawn. But 12.Nb5! was the key idea: it was a discovered attack, because the knight left c3 and your Bd2 hit the bishop on b4. After 12...cxb5 13.Bxb4 Qxd1+ 14.Rxd1 you were fine.
14...Nc6?? gave you +5.5, but 15.Rg4?? (engine 15.Rxe6+) threw it back to +0.3. The middlegame drifted to level, and 19.h4?! cost a little more.
Then Black went wrong with 22...Nb4?? and you found 23.Rd7!, then 23...Nxa2?? 24.Re7+!. Two rooks on the seventh finished it: 25.Rdd7 Nb4 26.Rxf7+ Kg8 27.Rg7#.

review.turning_point: 22...Nb4?? let you play 23.Rd7!, and two rooks on the seventh rank decided the game.
review.focus: 15.Rg4?? let a +5.5 position fall to +0.3. After 14...Nc6, check every capture and check first; 15.Rxe6+ was the engine move.

review.headline: A tidy win on the kingside, with some chances to finish it quicker

sections.text: Your ...e5 and ...d5 setup was already comfortable, and 8...e4 gained space (+1.8). The first real chance came with 11...Bxh3 12.gxh3, which wrecked White's kingside pawns, and 13...Nxg4 14.hxg4 left White with doubled g-pawns.
14...Qe7? (engine 14...f5) was an inaccuracy, but 15.Ne2 Qh4 16.Nf4? gave you the chance. You answered 16...g5!, and after 17.a5 gxf4 you were a piece up.
You kept winning material with 18...fxe3 and 22...Bxf4?!. You traded queens with 24...Qf3+ 25.Qxf3 exf3 26.Rxg3+ Kh7 27.Rxf3 e2, and the passed e-pawn became very dangerous.
33.Kg2? let you play on at +9.7, though 33...e1=N+?! gave back some of that. White's flag fell at move 34.

review.turning_point: 16.Nf4? g5! won a piece and broke White's kingside, giving you a winning attack.
review.focus: 14...Qe7? gave up part of your edge (+2.7 to +1.3). Before a quiet queen move, look for active ideas such as the engine's 14...f5, which kept the initiative.

review.headline: An Open Sicilian that turned in your favour, then slipped away on the clock

sections.text: This was a normal Open Sicilian until 8.Nb5? cost you the opening edge (+0.9 to -0.5). The engine preferred 8.Nc3. You then steadied it with 9.Nd4 and 10.Nxc6, but 13.O-O?! and 16.Qg4?! made your position uncomfortable (-1.0).
Black blundered with 19...e5??, which handed you +2.5, but you did not find the best reply. 20.f5? gave most of it back (+1.0), and 21.exd5?? (engine 21.Qh4) turned it into -1.7.
22...e4?? gave you a second chance (+0.3), but 23.Qf4?? (engine 23.Bg5) missed it. 24.Nxf5 Bxf5 and Black's pieces took over.
Low on time, 27.h5? missed 27.Be3, but you hit back with 28.Qxd6! after 27...Qd6??. The ending was fine for a while at about -0.7, until 34.Re2?? (-4.4), and you lost on time at move 36.

review.turning_point: 34.Re2?? dropped from -0.7 to -4.4 and let the d-pawn run.
review.focus: 27.h5? and 34.Re2?? both came in time trouble. In rook endings play the safe move, like 34.Kh2, instead of rushing a rook move.

review.headline: A good middlegame spoiled by a king move that walked into mate

sections.text: White avoided the main Petrov lines with 3.Bd3, and your setup of 3...d6?!, 5...c6 and 6...b6?! was passive but safe. 10.b5 c5? (engine 10...dxe4) let White open the centre with 11.exd5 Nxd5 12.Nxd5 Bxd5.

13.O-O?? was a real mistake by White (+2.1 for you), but 13...O-O?? missed the point. The engine's 13...e4 would have forked the bishop on d3 and the knight on f3 with the pawn, and you would have been better.

14.Nxe5 was a free pawn grab, and 14...Bd6?? was the wrong reply, since 14...Nxe5 was the right capture. You then found the best reply to 15.Nxd7? with 15...Qxd7!, and White's 16.Bxh7+?? gave you the chance to come back into the game.
Then came the fatal move. 16...Kh8?? (-7.6) allowed 17.Qh5, and the engine's 16...Kxh7 was the answer. After 17...Qb7 18.Be4+ Kg8 there was no defence to 19.Qh7#.

review.turning_point: 16...Kh8?? declined the free bishop on h7 and walked into 17.Qh5 and a mating attack.
review.focus: 16...Kh8?? should have been 16...Kxh7. When a piece checks you for free, first see whether you can simply take it, then check what its capture leaves open.

review.headline: A messy Italian saved by a well-timed knight trade and the clock

sections.text: 5.Bg5 f6 6.Bh4?! g5 7.Bg3 h5 8.h4 g4 was a messy pawn storm against your bishop, and the engine already preferred Black at -0.5. 10.Nc3?? (engine 10.exf5) allowed 10...f4 and made it worse (-2.3).

Black did not make the most of it. 11...Nd4? (engine 11...Qxh4) and 13...c6? gave you real counterplay. You answered with the key idea 14.Nxc5!, trading your offside knight for Black's active bishop, and the evaluation improved to -1.1.

After 15.c3 Ne2 16.d4 cxd4 17.Bxe2 fxe2 18.Qxe2 dxc3 19.bxc3 the knight was gone and queens were still on. You castled, and 22.Qe3?! O-O-O 23.Nb3 Bxb3 24.axb3 Rxd1+ 25.Rxd1 led to a roughly balanced ending.
25...Qa3? (engine 25...Rd8) was the final inaccuracy, and 26.b4 kept you in the game. You won on time.

review.turning_point: 14.Nxc5! traded off Black's strong bishop and let you escape the worst of the kingside attack.
review.focus: 10.Nc3?? let the f-pawn advance. 10.exf5 opened the position and kept Black's pawns in check. Take the pawn and deal with the tension at once.

review.headline: A Petrov Italian won by one tactic on move 15

sections.text: 3...Bc5?? was a slip in the opening (the engine liked 3...Nxe4), but 4.O-O? let you off the hook. You castled, answered 5.Nxe5 d6 6.Nf3 Nxe4, and were comfortable. 7.d4 Bb6 8.c3 Re8 9.Bd3 d5 followed.

11...Bg4?! and 12.Qc2 Nxd2? were not the best (the engine liked 12...Bxf3), but 12...Nxd2 was a discovered attack: the knight left e4 and your rook on e8 hit the bishop on e3. White replied 13.Nxd2? instead of 13.Bxh7+.
15.f4?? lost on the spot to 15...Rxe3!, and after 16.Bxg4 Qxg4 17.Rae1 Rxe1 18.Rxe1 you were a piece up (+5).
You converted with 20...Nf6, 21...Bxf4 and 23...Bxe5?!, and White's clock ran out at move 24.

review.turning_point: 15.f4?? allowed 15...Rxe3!, winning material that you held to the end.
review.focus: 3...Bc5?? let White take on e5 with tempo; 3...Nxe4 was the safe move. In the Petrov, take on e4 before developing the bishop.

review.headline: An early tactic won a knight, then a nervy ending with a queen race

sections.text: You played an Anti-Torre with 2...Bg4, traded off bishops with 5.Bxd6 Qxd6 and 8.Ne5 Bxe2, and the position stayed level through 13.Rfc1 c5. Then 14.c4?? let your queen in.
14...Qxa4! won a knight, and even after 15.dxc5 bxc5 you kept a clear edge, near +5 for most of the game. Your 20...dxc4 and 21...Rxd7 kept the position simple.
In the endgame the plan was clear until 44...Kd7?? (+6.6 to -3.5): the engine wanted 44...exf5+. You were suddenly worse, but White's 47.Kf4?? gave it back and 47...c4! got your pawn running.
You queened with 50...c1=Q+ and your queen did the rest. 53...Qg4+? let a forced mate slip, but 54...Qc4+! kept the win, and 61...Qa7# ended it.

review.turning_point: 14.c4?? allowed 14...Qxa4!, and you won a knight with a lasting advantage.
review.focus: 44...Kd7?? let a +6.6 ending slip to -3.5. Look at pawn captures first; 44...exf5+ kept everything simple.

review.headline: A Philidor that went from +4.5 to a drawn rook ending after one slip

sections.text: In the Philidor you took on d4 with 5.Nxd4, then went for the queen swap with 7.e5 dxe5 8.Qxd8+ Bxd8 9.Nxe5, and the game was level. 12.Bf4? (engine 12.Nxc6) let Black trade with 12...Nxe5 13.Bxe5, and after 14.f4 Bxe5 15.Rxe5 Rxe5 16.fxe5 it was still equal.
Black blundered with 16...Bf5??, and you found 17.exf6!. After 17...Bxc2 18.fxg7 you had a strong passed pawn on g7 and were +4.2.

Then came 21.Na4??, a blunder that dropped the evaluation to 0.0. The engine's 21.Kf2 kept the edge. After 21...b5 22.Nxc5 bxc4 23.Nxa6 you still had some material (+2), but Black's pieces were active enough to equalise.
26.Rf4?! Bd3? and 27.Nxd3? (engine 27.Kf2) were more slips. The rook ending was balanced, and after 48.Kg1 Ra1+ 49.Kh2 Ra2 the game finished as a draw.

review.turning_point: 21.Na4?? let a +4.6 advantage drop to zero.
review.focus: 21.Na4?? sent the knight to the rim and gave away a +4.6 edge. When well ahead, make the quiet, safe move like the engine's 21.Kf2 instead of looking for more.

review.headline: A Scandinavian attack that fell apart, then won with a back-rank mate

sections.text: You met the Scandinavian with 2.exd5 Qxd5 3.Nc3 Qe5+ 4.Be2 and grabbed space with 5.h3 and 6.g4, kicking the bishop to g6. 7.Nf3 Qa5 8.d4 Nc6 9.Bd2 O-O-O had you at +2.8, a very comfortable position.

11.Ne5?? threw most of that away (+2.8 to -0.9), and the engine preferred the quiet 11.a4. After 11...Nxe5 12.dxe5 e6, 13.Be3?? was worse: it was a discovered attack, because moving the bishop off d2 let Black's rook on d8 hit your queen on d1.
You were down material after 14.Rxd1 Bc5 15.Bxc5 Qxc5, with the engine at -4.4, and you kept making simple developing moves such as 16.O-O, 17.Rd2 and 18.Rfd1.
Black's 19...Nf4?? was the blunder that lost the game, because the knight left d5 and uncovered your rook on d2. You found 20.Rxd8#, a back rank mate with the king stuck on c8.

review.turning_point: 19...Nf4?? let you play 20.Rxd8#, ending a game you were losing.
review.focus: 13.Be3?? moved the bishop that blocked the d-file. Before moving a piece, ask what it is shielding. 13.O-O was the safe move.

review.headline: A messy Scandinavian with big swings and a drawn finish on the clock

sections.text: Against a much lower-rated opponent you played 3.Nc3?! and 5.Bb5?, which let Black equalise. 6.Qf3? Bb4 7.Bd2 O-O was fine, but 8.Nxd5?? was a real mistake (-3.5), though Black replied 8...exd5?? and gave it back.
You built an attack with 13.Ng3, 14.h4, 15.Nh5 and 16.Qg4, and Black cracked at 17...Bc8?? (+3.0). But 18.Qg3?? and 19.c3?? threw it all away (-2.7). The engine wanted 18.Qf4 and 19.Qe3.

More swings followed: 21.Kc2? (-4.5), then 22.Nxg6?! b1=Q+, which forked your king and rook. 23.Kd2?? allowed a forced mate, when 23.Rxb1 was the answer. Black missed it, queens came off with 24.Qxg6+ fxg6, and you were still worse.

In the ending, 35.Rxf5+! and 36.Re5+! turned things around: 36.Re5+ was a skewer of king and rook, and 37.Rxe8 won the rook. You were +8.7 by move 40, but 42.Kg5?? (low on time) dropped to 0.0, and the game was recorded as a draw on time after 52...Kd4.

review.turning_point: 42.Kg5?? turned a +8.7 pawn ending into a draw while you were low on time.
review.focus: 42.Kg5?? ignored 42.dxc5. When you are winning in a pawn ending, take the pawn that removes counterplay first.

review.headline: A Petrov against a much higher-rated player that went wrong on move 14

sections.text: You played the Petrov well against a 1582. After 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.Nc3 Nxc3 6.dxc3 d5 7.Bd3 Bc5 the position was equal, and 8.O-O O-O 9.Ng5 g6 10.Nf3 Bg4 11.Bh6 Re8 kept it that way.
12.h3 hit your bishop, and 12...Bc8? (-1.2) retreated instead of 12...Bxf3. 13.b4 Bb6?! (-1.5) was another small step back.
14.c4 d4?? was the decisive mistake (-5.1). The engine's 14...c6 15.Qd2 was far better. After 15.c5 Nc6 16.cxb6 axb6, you were down material (-2).
You fought on with 19...Qh4 and 23...Re2, but White kept things simple. With 27...Rxc4?! and 28...Rcc2?! you ran out of time around 29.Qd8+.

review.turning_point: 14...d4?? dropped a bishop and went from -1.5 to -5.1.
review.focus: 12...Bc8? passed on 12...Bxf3. When a bishop is attacked and you can trade it for a knight, capture, as the engine's 12...Bxf3 13.Qxf3 Nc6 did.

review.headline: A wild Van Geet game you won on time after throwing away a big edge

sections.text: Against a 1685 you played the sharp 3...Nc6? (engine 3...e4), but White's 4.Nf3?? was a blunder and you found 4...e4!. After 5.Ne5 Nxe5 6.dxe5 f6?? (-1.6) White replied 7.exf6??, and you took 7...Nxf6! with a fine game.
10...b6?? was another loosener (engine 10...Be7), but 11.a3?? let you play 11...Be7!. 12.f3 Bb7? 13.fxe4 Nxe4 14.Nxe4 dxe4 left the position about level.

Then came the game's best move. After 17.Qh5??, you found 17...Bxc3!, a discovered attack: the bishop left f6 and your rook on f8 hit the rook on f1. 18.bxc3 Qd2 19.Rad1 Qxe3+ 20.Kh1 Rxf1+ 21.Rxf1 Qxc3 put you at +2.4.
23.Qxc7?? hit your bishop and gave you +4.8, but 23...e3?? threw it all away (-4.7). The engine's 23...Ba6 was the move. You were down for the rest of the game, but won when White flagged at move 39.

review.turning_point: 17...Bxc3! won material with a discovered attack, but 23...e3?? gave the whole edge back.
review.focus: 23...e3?? pushed a pawn while the bishop on b7 was hanging. Before pushing, check which piece is attacked; 23...Ba6 was the engine's move.

review.headline: A Stonewall-style game won by a sharp rook sacrifice

sections.text: White played a slow 4.f4 Stonewall setup and you answered with 5...c5 6.c3 c4, gaining space. 8.Ne5 Nxe5?! 9.fxe5 Nd7 was fine, but 10...f6? (engine 10...O-O) and 11.exf6? Nxf6 left you worse (-1.7).
12.O-O? gave you a chance and 12...O-O! took it, but 13...b6?? (engine 13...e5) dropped you to -2.9 and allowed 14.e5 and 15.Qh5 g6?!. After 16.Bxg6 you were facing a kingside attack.
Here you found 16...Rxf1+!. 17.Kxf1?? Qf8+! and 18.Kg1?? hxg6! brought you back into the game, and 19.Qxg6+ Qg7 20.Qxe6+ Kh8 left you ready to counter.
21.Nf3?? (engine 21.Qc6) let you play 21...Nc5!, a discovered attack on the queen on e6. 22.Qh6+ Qxh6 23.Bxh6 Ne4 and White resigned after 24.Rf1.

review.turning_point: 16...Rxf1+! started a forcing sequence that turned a worse position into a winning one.
review.focus: 13...b6?? weakened your queenside and dropped to -2.9. Prefer 13...e5, which challenges the centre instead of waiting.

review.headline: Petrov game with a shaky opening, a steady middlegame and a forced finish on the f-file

sections.text: After 4.Bc4 Be6 5.Bxe6 fxe6 you had an open f-file and a solid centre. White's knight excursions with 6.Ng5 and 8.Nh3 were awkward, and you stood a little better (+0.9) after 8.Nh3.

Then you gave it back. 8...c6 was a small slip, and 9...d5 was the real mistake (-2.2): you opened the centre at a moment when White was ready to punish it, and the engine preferred 9...g5. White answered with 10.f3, which put the evaluation back near zero. The stronger 10.f4 would have kept the pressure on.

Your middlegame play was good. 14.fxe5 opened the f-file and uncovered a discovered attack by the rook on your knight, but 14...Nxe5! was exactly the right reply and your pieces came to life. After the exchanges on f6 and f1 you traded a pair of rooks and kept a healthy position.

White's 20.c3 was the blunder that decided things. 20...Nxd3! won a pawn and left the d3 knight a thorn in White's position (+3.2). After 21.Qb3 Qf6, 22.c4 uncovered an attack on your knight, but 22...Qf2+ was far stronger and the engine finds a forced mate from there.

review.turning_point: 20.c3 let you play 20...Nxd3!, winning a pawn and planting a monster knight; 22...Qf2+ then ended the game.
review.focus: Before pushing a central pawn like 9...d5, check White's forcing replies such as 10.f4 and count what your uncastled king is exposed to. The engine preferred 9...g5 there.

review.headline: Rousseau Gambit where a bad grab on move 4 was rescued when Black blundered back

sections.text: Black went for the Rousseau Gambit with 3...f5, and 4.Nxe5?? (+1.1 down to -2.6) took the pawn but lost the knight to 4...Nxe5. The engine wanted the quiet 4.d3. 5.exf5?! kept you a little behind after that.

Credit to you for staying calm, because Black returned the favour at once. 6...Bd6?? swung the evaluation from -3.9 to +1.5, and you found 7.d4!, hitting the knight on e5. The queens came off and you were a pawn up.

After 10.O-O d5 11.Re1, Black's 11...Ng4?? gave you the game (+4.9). 12.h3! was the right idea, and after 12...Bxf5 13.hxg4 dxc4 14.Rxe5+ you had picked up the knight and the bishop and were far ahead.
The rest was technique. 15.Rxf5, 16.Rf7+ and 18.Rxc7+ kept Black's king under fire. 27.Rb6 gave back some of the edge (+8.9 to +6.4) and 32.Re3?! was a little loose, but the win was never in danger.

review.turning_point: 6...Bd6?? by Black, which you punished with 7.d4! after being a piece down.
review.focus: On 4.Nxe5 the engine preferred 4.d3. Against a gambit like 3...f5, check whether the grabbed pawn can be recaptured before you take it.

review.headline: Bishop's Opening where White overreached, you drifted, and a queen blunder swing decided it

sections.text: White's early queen play with 3.Qh5 and 4.Qf3, followed by the pawn storm 6.g4 and 7.g5, left you comfortably better (+2.2 after 7.g5). You developed sensibly and castled quickly.

You then let the edge fade with 7...Nfd7?! and 8...Nb6?!. After 9.b3? you traded off the bishop with 9...Nxc4 10.bxc4, which wrecked White's pawns. 11...Bb7? was a mistake (the engine liked 11...Nc6) and 14...Nd4? left you slightly worse (-1.7).

Both sides then blundered. 15.Na3 missed 15.Qxh7+, but 15...Qd7?? (-5.1) put your queen where the same capture on h7 came with tempo, and 16.Qxd7 was the strong reply. White instead played 16.Qxh7+??, and 16...Kf7! was the only move that held everything together.
18.Qxg7+? was a queen sacrifice that did not work, and 18...Kxg7! took the queen. From there 19.Nb5 Nxb5 20.cxb5 Qg4 and 24...Qxf2+ and 26...Qxe2 were clean, and you finished well ahead on material.

review.turning_point: 15...Qd7?? looked natural but was a big blunder (-5.1); White missed the punishment, and your 16...Kf7! turned the position back in your favour.
review.focus: On 15...Qd7 you moved the queen without checking White's checks and captures. Before every queen move, look at 16.Qxh7+ style forcing moves. The engine preferred 15...Qc8.

review.headline: Latvian Gambit where you fumbled the opening but Black's blunders handed you a queen

sections.text: Black's 2...f5? is the Latvian Gambit, and the engine liked 3.Nxe5. 3.d3? and 4.g3? let Black equalise, and 5.exf5?! and 6.Bg5?! kept you slightly worse (-1.3). 6.Bg5 did pin the knight on f6 to the queen on d8, which gave you some activity.
Black's 7...e4?? was the turning point. 8.dxe4! dxe4 was the right way to take advantage, but 9.Bxf6? gave back most of the edge (+2.0 down to +0.8). The engine's 9.Qxd6 Bxd6 was clearly stronger.

Black then blundered again with 10...gxf6??. Their 10...Qe6+ would have forked king and bishop on f6, but you took a pawn with 11.Qxb7. Then 11...Qc6? set a fork of its own, hitting your queen on b7 and the rook on h1, and your answer 12.Bb5! pinned the queen to the king on e8.
That one move won the game. You took 13.Qxa8 and 14.Qxb8+, and 15.Bxc6 traded your bishop for their queen, leaving you far ahead.

review.turning_point: 12.Bb5! pinned the queen on c6 to the king, so Black could not keep both queen and rooks safe.
review.focus: 9.Bxf6? recaptured too quickly. The engine's 9.Qxd6 Bxd6 would have won a piece. Before taking, look for a stronger in-between capture.

review.headline: A good position thrown away by two mistakes, then lost on the clock

sections.text: You set up a solid Queen's Gambit style structure with pawns on d5, e6 and c6 and pieces behind them. White built pressure with 7.Qc2, 8.Ng5 and 9.h4, all of it aimed at your kingside.
9...hxg5?? took a knight but opened the h-file towards your king, and after 10.hxg5 your knight on f6 was under attack (-1.7). The engine preferred the calm 9...Re8.

White returned the favour straight away. 11.Nxd5?? uncovered an attack from the bishop on b2 onto your knight, but 11...exd5?! and 12.gxf6?? left White worse. Your 12...Bxf6! pinned the b2 bishop to the rook on a1 and put you well ahead (+3.1).

You were still clearly better (+3.2) after 14.Bd3, but 14...Nb6?? threw away most of that edge (+0.6) and allowed 15.Bxg6. The engine preferred 14...Bg7. The game then ended on the clock after 15 moves, with you still a pawn up.

review.turning_point: 14...Nb6?? cut your advantage from +3.2 to +0.6, and the clock then ended a game you were still doing fine in.
review.focus: When you are ahead, reach for the safe consolidating move such as 14...Bg7 and keep an eye on the clock. This game ended on time with you still ahead.

review.headline: Opposite-side castling where your pawn storm beat White's slow queenside defence

sections.text: A calm Petrov where you put your bishop on g4 with 4...Bg4 and kept things sensible. 6...Bh5?! was a little loose, because after 6.h3 the engine simply liked 6...Bxf3 7.Bxf3. White castled long with 10.O-O-O, and you started a pawn storm on that side.

11.Na4? was White's first mistake, and 11...b5! chased the knight at once. 12.Nc3 a4 13.a3 b4?! was a touch early (the engine preferred 13...Rb8), but White's 14.Na2?? was a real blunder. 14.axb4 d5 was the engine's choice.
You punished it with 14...bxa3!, which won a pawn and tore open the king. After 15.bxa3 d5, 16.exd5? made it worse and 16...Bxa3+! was strong, giving you +7.1.
The finish was tidy. 18.Nb4 Bxb4 won a knight and 19.Qc1 Ba3+ kept the king under pressure. White resigned soon after.

review.turning_point: 14.Na2?? allowed 14...bxa3!, and White's king never recovered.
review.focus: After 6.h3 you retreated with 6...Bh5?!, but the engine preferred to trade right away with 6...Bxf3. When the bishop on g4 is questioned, trade it rather than retreat it unless you have a concrete reason.

review.headline: Long Philidor where you built a big edge, threw it away, then fought back and let a won ending slip to a draw

sections.text: A good start for you. After 8.Nf5 Bxf5 9.exf5 and 11.Nd5 bxc4? Black took a bishop, but 12.Nxe7+! won the other bishop back with check. 13.Bg5 and 14.Qxd6 followed, and you were comfortably better (+2.3).

You kept control with 15.Re2 and 16.Rae1. 17.Ng6+?! was a discovered attack, because the knight check uncovered Re2 on the rook on e8. It worked well enough, and after 19.Bxd8 Rxd6 20.Rxe8+ and 21.fxg6+ fxg6 you were still clearly ahead (+3.1).

Then came two blunders. 22.g3?? allowed 22...Rd1+, and after 23.Kg2 Nf6 your bishop on d8 was attacked. 24.Re7?? ignored that, and 24...Rxd8 dropped the bishop (-3.5). The engine wanted 24.Bxf6. Black's extra material and c-pawn made the next phase hard.
You fought back well. 36...Rb2?? let you in, 37.a7! was the right reply, and 38...Rxb6?? allowed 39.a8=Q!. A queen against a rook should be winning (+4.2 around move 43).
57.Kf3?? let Black play 57...Rf5, and 58.Qxf5 gxf5 left a drawn pawn ending; the game ended with bare kings.

review.turning_point: 57.Kf3?? let Black give up the rook for your queen with 57...Rf5, reaching a drawn pawn ending when you were winning.
review.focus: With a queen against a rook, avoid king moves like 57.Kf3 that allow a queen-for-rook trade. The engine preferred 57.Qg5, keeping the queen active.

review.headline: Wild Philidor where both sides blundered and your attack just outlasted theirs

sections.text: 4.Ng5?! was a speculative idea, and 5...Nxd5?? by Black uncovered the queen on d8 onto your knight with a discovered attack. 6.Nxf7?! forked the queen and rook on d8 and h8, but after 6...Kxf7 you had sacrificed a knight for a pawn. The idea worked because Black's king was exposed (+0.7).

7.Qf3+ Ke6 8.Nc3 c6 9.O-O Na6 10.Re1 Nb4 gave you a strong attack (+2.8). But 11.Qe4?? and 12.Qxe5+?? threw away much of it, and then 13.Nxb5?? lost the plot (-1.3). The engine wanted 13.Nxd5 Nxd5 14.Bxd5.
Black blundered right back. 12...Kd7?? (the engine suggested 12...Kf7) and 13...cxb5?? let you in. 14.Bxb5+! was the key move and put you at +7.4.

You then let the lead shrink. 16.Qc4?, 17.Re8?? and 18.Qe4?? gave away most of your edge (+5.0 down to +0.6), and Black's 20...Nxd4?? gave you the edge again. 21.Bf4+? was imprecise, but 21...Kd8?? let you finish with 22.Qxa8+! and 23.Qd5+.

review.turning_point: 13...cxb5?? and then 14.Bxb5+! flipped the game from -1.3 to +7.4 in one exchange.
review.focus: After 16.Qc4? and 17.Re8??, you stopped developing. The engine's 17.d3 would have kept all your pieces working. When you are winning, finish development before looking for the next tactic.

review.headline: A good attacking fight ruined by an early positional loss and a late queen blunder

sections.text: 3...d6?! was slightly loose, and 4.Ng5 hit f7. 4...Be6?? let White trade on e6, and 5.Bxe6 fxe6 6.Nxe6 cost you a pawn (the evaluation fell to -1.7 after 4...Be6). The engine preferred 4...d5 5.exd5.

You got the pawn back with 8...Nxe4 and the game balanced out. 11...O-O-O and a kingside pawn storm (13...g5?!, 15...g4, 16...h5, 17...h4) was a sensible plan against White's own queenside pawns, though 14...Be7? and 19...Qxf6? (the engine liked 19...Bxf6) were small slips.
Then White blundered. 20.g3?? was a blunder, and your 20...hxg3! put you at +6.6.
But 21...Qh6?? threw it all away (+6.7 to -3.9). The engine's 21...Rxh2 22.Ra2 Rxa2 kept your attack going. You resigned a few moves later.

review.turning_point: 21...Qh6?? turned a winning attack (+6.7) into a losing position (-3.9). 21...Rxh2 was the move.
review.focus: 4...Be6?? walked into a bishop trade that cost you a pawn after 6.Nxe6. When White aims a knight and bishop at f7, defend solidly with 4...d5 as the engine suggested.

review.headline: Italian game where you got worse in the middlegame, then won with a trap and a mating net

sections.text: A quiet Giuoco Pianissimo: 4.d3 Bb6 5.Be3 Bxe3 6.fxe3 gave you a half-open f-file. You castled and developed with 7.O-O and 8.Nc3, and the position was level after 9.h3 Bh5 10.g4 Bg6.

Then the pawn advances went wrong. 11.g5?! and 12.h4?! loosened your king, and 13.d4? (the engine preferred 13.Kf2) opened the centre. 14.dxe5?? was the real blunder (-3.4), and 14.Nxg5 would have used a discovered attack of the queen on the knight on h5.
Black's attack then ran strong: 15...Nxe5, 16...Ng3 and 17...Rxh4 put you well behind (-4.9 at 18.Qd5). But 18.Qd5 set a trap, and 19...Rxa1?? fell for it. The engine suggested 19...Qxg5.
You punished it perfectly: 20.Nxf7! Nxf7?? 21.Rxf7! and after 21...Qh4? came 22.Qe6+!, which forked the king on e8 and the bishop on g6, and 23.Qd7# ended it.

review.turning_point: 19...Rxa1?? by Black, which you punished at once with 20.Nxf7!, turning a lost position into a winning attack.
review.focus: 14.dxe5?? was the key error; the engine's 14.Nxg5 used a discovered attack on the knight. Before capturing a pawn, check if another capture also uncovers an attack.

review.headline: Short Petrov game that ended on the clock after only nine moves

sections.text: Against the higher-rated opponent you played a solid Petrov: 4...Bg4 and 5...c6 were fine, and the position was close to equal (-0.4) after 5...c6. 6...h5?! was a bit optimistic (-1.1), but White's 7.Nd2 did not take advantage.
8.f4? was White's mistake and gave you a chance. The engine liked 8...exf4. 8...g6? let White off the hook (-0.7), and 9.h3 came next. You were not worse by much.
The game then ended on the clock after only nine moves, so there was no time to see how it would have gone.

review.turning_point: 8.f4? gave you a chance to take advantage, but 8...g6? let White off instead of 8...exf4.
review.focus: After 8.f4? the engine's 8...exf4 was the move to punish it. Also, since this game ended on time after nine moves, work on making your opening choices quicker.

review.headline: Long Petrov game decided in the endgame, where you went from worse to winning to a draw

sections.text: A normal Petrov with 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4. 8...Bg4? pinned the f3 knight against the queen on e2 (-1.3), but the engine preferred 8...Nc5. White's 9.d3? gave the edge back, and after 10.Qxe7+ Bxe7 the queens were off.
16...Nd3? was a mistake (the engine liked 16...Nxc4), but White's 17.c5?? gave it back. 18...Nxc1 19.Raxc1 traded your knight for a bishop, and the position was roughly level.

The endgame went wrong. 33...d4?? (-3.4) was a blunder, and the engine preferred 33...Kf7. 35.Kf2?? let you back in, but 35...Ke7?? gave it away again (the engine preferred 35...Ba5). 39.Nxc3?? dxc3! then reached an equal king and pawn ending.
46.Kf2?? was a big gift (+5.6), and you played 46...Kf5 and 48...Kg5 well. But 50...g6?? threw away the win.
The engine preferred 50...Kg6, keeping your king in front of your pawns. After 50...g6 the game ended in a draw.

review.turning_point: 50...g6?? in a won king and pawn ending (+5.8). 50...Kg6 was the move.
review.focus: In king and pawn endings, keep the king active and count tempi. 50...g6 spent a pawn move when 50...Kg6 was winning.

review.headline: Bird's Opening where early gifts went to waste and your dark squares fell apart

sections.text: A decent start: 4...Nxe5 5.fxe5 was an even trade of knights. 5...Nd7?! was a little passive, but White's 7.exd5?? gave you a clear edge (+1.8).
7...exd5?? threw that away (-0.5), when 7...Qh4+ was the move. Then White's 9.Bd3?? gave you another chance, and 9...Bb4 pinned the c3 knight to the king on e1, but 9...Qh4+ was the engine's move.

11...Bxc3+?? was the key mistake (-4.1). Your dark-squared bishop was the main defender of the dark squares around your king, which White's queen and bishop were already eyeing. The engine preferred 11...Bf8.
After that 14...b6? and 15...Qg7?! did not help, and 16...O-O walked into 17.Bh6 with a lost position (-7.5).

review.turning_point: 11...Bxc3+?? gave up the bishop that guarded your dark squares, and White's queen and bishop swarmed your king.
review.focus: 7...exd5 and 9...Bb4 both missed the check 7...Qh4+ and 9...Qh4+. When White's king is stuck in the centre and pawns have moved, look for queen checks first.

review.headline: Two Knights line where you punished one slip with clean, accurate play

sections.text: A model game against a lower-rated opponent. You played the open Two Knights lines with 4.d4 and 5.exd5 and kept the extra pawn after 6.dxe5.

Black played 6...Nxe5??, and 7.Nxe5! was the right answer, winning a knight (+5.2) while your bishop on c4 kept the pressure on d5. 8.Qf3?! was a small slip (the engine liked 8.O-O), but it did not matter.
After 8...Bb4+ 9.c3 Qf6 you went 10.Bxd5, and 10...O-O-O? allowed 11.Qxf6 gxf6 12.Bxe6+ fxe6 13.cxb4 fxe5, leaving you comfortably ahead.
You converted with 14.O-O, 15.Bg5 and 16.Bf6. 17.Bxe5 won another pawn, and 24.Nd6+ Kd8 25.Nxb5+ picked up the rook. Black resigned.

review.turning_point: 6...Nxe5?? by Black, answered by 7.Nxe5!, left you a piece up (+5.2).
review.focus: 8.Qf3?! was the only slip. The engine preferred 8.O-O to castle first. Even when winning, develop before bringing the queen out.

review.headline: Stafford Gambit where you took the pawn, weakened your own king, and Black blundered twice

sections.text: You answered the Stafford Gambit well: 3.Nxe5 Nc6? 4.Nxc6! dxc6 left you a pawn up (+1.8). The engine suggested 3...d6 as better for Black.
Then you drifted. 6.Be3? (the engine preferred 6.Be2) let Black trade it off with 6...Bxe3 7.fxe3, doubling your pawns. 8.Qe2?! and 9.h3 Qh4+ 10.Kd2 left your king in the centre.
11.g3? and 12.Bg2?? were your biggest errors. 12.Bg2 dropped to -4.2, and the engine wanted 12.Kc1. But Black's 12...O-O-O?? gave it straight back, and you found 13.Nc3!.
14...Qe7?? let you take a knight with 15.dxc4! and you were clearly ahead. 17.Rxd8+ Rxd8 and 19.Kb2 completed the consolidation, and you won on time.

review.turning_point: 14...Qe7?? by Black allowed 15.dxc4!, winning a knight.
review.focus: Your king on d2 after 10.Kd2 caused trouble. The engine's 11.Qe1 and 12.Kc1 would have gotten it to safety. When forced to move the king, get it off the open centre quickly.

review.headline: Halasz-McDonnell Gambit where White overreached and your tactics on the long diagonal and the king finished it

sections.text: White's 3.f4? was a mistake, and 3...Nc6! was the right reply. You held the pawn after 4.Nf3 d5 5.e5 f6, and 7...fxe5 won a pawn (+2 material) even though 6...Bd7?! was a little passive.

review.turning_point: 12...Bg7! skewered White's queen and knight, which won a piece after 13.Qg5??.
review.focus: 10...Rg8?? was a big slip. The engine preferred 10...Qd7. After a gambit line, finish development before moving rooks.

review.headline: A well-played Queen's Gambit Declined that you gave up while it was roughly level

sections.text: A very accurate game from you (accuracy 95.9, no mistakes). You met 3.cxd5 with 3...exd5 and developed naturally: 5...Bd6, 6...c6 and 7...Bg4.
8.h3 Bxf3 9.Qxf3 O-O was a standard trade. White started a pawn storm with 10.g4 and 12.g5, and you responded sensibly with 11...Re8 and 12...Ne4, breaking its momentum.
13.Nxe4 dxe4 14.Bxe4 took a pawn, but 14...Qxg5 got it back at once, and the engine rated the position as only slightly worse for you (-0.5).
That makes the resignation after 15.Bd2 a surprise. There was nothing lost in that position and plenty of game left.

review.turning_point: The game ended by resignation after 15.Bd2 in a position that was only about -0.5. Nothing was decided yet.
review.focus: After 15.Bd2 you were only slightly worse and had just regained the pawn with 14...Qxg5. Keep playing until the position really tells you otherwise.

sections.text: You played the Scandinavian with 2.exd5 Qxd5 3.Nc3 and calm development: 4.d4, 5.Nf3, 6.Be2 and 8.Bf4. You got both bishops after 6...Bxf3 7.Bxf3 and slowly improved, with 9.O-O and 10.Re1.

sections.text: You chose the open Two Knights with 4.d4, and after 4...Nxe4 5.Nxe5 d5 the game was fine. 6.Nxc6?! bxc6 was a slight concession; 6.Bb5 pins the c6 knight to the king and keeps more tension.

review.focus: At 17...f5 you missed a forcing shot; look at forks like 17...Ne3 first, and keep an eye on the clock when you are better.

review.focus: With your king still in the centre, 16.g5? opened lines against yourself; 16.Ke2 was calmer.

Taking on h7 won a bishop on paper, but it pulled your king into the attack.

review.focus: At 13...Kxh7 you accepted a sacrifice that opened your king; 13...Kh8 was safer. When a piece lands next to your castled king, check the queen routes first.

sections.text: This was a Leonardis Variation of the King's Pawn Game. You developed naturally: 3...d6 4.Nc3 Nc6 5.Bg5 Be7 was fine.

review.focus: At 17.Rh2?? you moved a rook while the bishop on g5 was hanging; 17.Be3 would have kept your edge.

At move 34, 34.Qc1? was inaccurate; 34.Qe8+ is a back rank check that would have kept the pressure. The game ended in perpetual check with 39.Qf5+ and 40.Qc8+, a draw despite a clear edge.

sections.text: 3.Nc3 d6 4.d4 exd4 5.Nxd4 Be7 6.Bc4 O-O 7.O-O Bd7 8.Bg5 Nc6 9.Nxc6 Bxc6 10.Re1 h6 11.Bh4 Qd7 was fine.
12.Bd5?? was a blunder, and 12...b6?? missed 12...Nxd5, a discovered attack with the bishop on e7 against h4.
After 13.Bxc6 Qxc6 14.Nd5, 14...Nxd5? was a blunder (14...Rae8 was best): 15.exd5 Qd7 16.Rxe7 won a bishop, and 16...Qg4? lost the queen to 17.Qxg4.

review.turning_point: 12...b6?? missed 12...Nxd5, and 14...Nxd5? lost a bishop.
review.focus: At 12...b6 you missed a free shot; 12...Nxd5 was a discovered attack.

review.headline: Anti-Fried Liver Italian won by a clean punishment
