Low on time, you missed 30.Bd8#, playing 30.Nc4+ instead. Then 33.Bg3?? moved the bishop off the h-file and let Black's rook on h2 hit your rook on h7, although Black missed it with 33...Kc4. You were +8 at move 40, but the clock ended the game.

review.turning_point: 29.cxb5+ followed by 30.Bd8# was a forced mate, but you played 30.Nc4+ instead and the game dragged on.
review.focus: Time: you missed 30.Bd8# and then 33.Be7+ because of the clock. In a winning position, look for forcing checks first.

review.headline: A clean, accurate win with the black pieces against the Chigorin

sections.text: You met 1.d4 with a Chigorin set-up and followed the plan well. After 3.Nc3 e6 4.Bf4 Bd6 5.e3 Bxf4 6.exf4 you gave White doubled f-pawns, and 9...Nxd3+ 10.Qxd3 removed White's best bishop.

White started losing the thread with 12.g4, 13.Qd2 and 14.Qd1, and then 15.a4? gave you the chance. 15...Bxe2! was a fork on d1, e2 and f3 that won a knight, and after 16.Qxe2 Qxf4 you were also a pawn up.
19.f3? was a second error, and 19...Ng3! was another fork, this time on the queen on e2 and the rook on h1. After 20.Qg2 Nxh1 21.Qxh1 Qh4+ you came out well ahead on material.

You kept your lead with 22...b5 and 23...bxa4 (slightly inaccurate, since the engine preferred 22...e5 and 23...Qf2+), but it did not matter: 24.Nxe6, 25.Nxc7 and 27...Rxc2 left White without defence, and he resigned at move 31.

review.turning_point: 19...Ng3! forked the queen and rook, converting a good position into a winning one (+3.8 to +5.3).
review.focus: Your opening choice 3...e6 was the least accurate; the engine liked 3...Bg4 to develop with more bite, and you could try it next time.

review.headline: A tricky trap in the Bishop's Opening that you missed, and then missed twice more

sections.text: You had a sound position in the Bishop's Opening: after 4.Bxe6 fxe6 5.Nf3 Nf6 6.d3 Nbd7 you were fine. White played the dubious 9.Ng5?, and you had a good answer.
Instead 9...Nh5?? left a piece to be won, with the engine preferring 9...Nxe4. After 10.Nxe6 Bxh4 11.Nxd8 Bxf2+ you were down heavily, though the position was still messy.

Then White blundered with 15.Nc3??, and you had a big chance. 15...Nxh1 would have won material, but you played 15...Bxc3+. Another chance came at 16.bxc3 and again 16...Nxh1 was winning; 16...Re2+ let White simplify with 17.Qxe2.
After that you were far behind, and White converted with 18.Kxe2, 24.Rd6 and 35.Kxe3. You resigned after 44.c6.

review.turning_point: 15...Bxc3+ and 16...Re2+ both missed the capture 15...Nxh1 (or 16...Nxh1), the knight on g3 taking the rook on h1, which would have turned the game around.
review.focus: At 16...Re2+, stop and look at all captures. The knight on g3 attacked the rook on h1 and 16...Nxh1 was the strongest move.

review.headline: A short Scotch-style win where Black grabbed a bishop's worth of trouble

sections.text: After 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 you were rewarded when Black played the dubious 2...Bc5. You could have simply taken on e5 with 3.Nxe5, but 3.d4 was a mistake that cut the advantage from +1.7 to +0.3.
Still, you traded in the centre well: 3...exd4 4.Nxd4 Nc6 5.Be3 Nxd4 6.Bxd4. Black then blundered with 6...Bb6??, ignoring 6...Bxd4. You found the right answer immediately.
7.Bxg7! took the pawn and attacked the rook on h8, so Black was in trouble. After 8.Bxh8 Bxf2+ 9.Kxf2 Nxe4+ you stayed ahead in material and moved your king back with 10.Ke1.
Black tried 10...Qh4+, but 11.g3 Nxg3 12.hxg3 Qxh1 left the king alone. 13.Qe2+ forced 13...Kd8, and 14.Bf6# finished the game.

review.turning_point: 6...Bb6 allowed 7.Bxg7!, winning a pawn and then the rook on h8.
review.focus: At 3.d4 you gave up a good position by opening too early. Look for 3.Nxe5, the simple capture, before pushing the d-pawn.

review.headline: A solid opening that fell apart after 12.Nxf6 and a sacrificed bishop on h6

sections.text: You played the Van't Kruijs with a flexible set-up: 1.e3 e5 2.e4, 3.d3, 4.Nf3 and 5.Be3. 10.Bg5 pinned the knight on f6 to the queen on e7 and you reached +1.3 after 11.Nd5.

Then you went wrong. 12.Nxf6 gxf6 gave Black a damaged but sturdy structure, while 12.Bxf6 gxf6 was the better route. After that 13.Bxh6 dropped the evaluation to -3.6, because 13.Be3 was the safe move.

Black used the open g-file and the queen on h3: 14.g3 Qh3 15.Be3 Bg4 pointed at your king, and 16.Nh4? was the final error, opening a discovered attack along the line from e2 to g4. After 16...Bxe2 you lost more material.
17.Qxe2 Rxh4 18.Bxb6 Qxh2# finished the game. Black's attack was straightforward once your pawn cover was gone.

review.turning_point: 13.Bxh6 grabbed a pawn but swung the evaluation from -0.5 to -3.6.
review.focus: At 12.Nxf6 and 13.Bxh6 you took material that opened your own king. Before capturing, check what the capture does to your kingside defence.

review.headline: A chaotic game where you won with bold tactics and a mating finish

sections.text: You played the Philidor-style set-up with 2...d6 and 3...Be6. After 4.Bxe6 fxe6 5.c3 Nf6 6.d4 exd4 7.cxd4 Nxe4 you grabbed a pawn and had a comfortable game.

The turning point came with a strong tactical sequence: 14.Nxd5 Bxb2 15.Rab1 Rxf3! was a brave exchange, and after 16.Rxb2 Qg5 17.Rxb7? Qxd5! you were back on top. White then overreached with 18.Rxc7?? and you found 18...Rc3!.
You nearly spoiled it with 21...Re7??, where 21...Qe5 was needed. White could have used 22.Rc8+ but played 22.Qc8+, a back rank check that you simply dodged with 22...Kf7!.
23.Rxe7+ Nxe7! was another great reply, and you closed in with 24.Qh8 Rc2. After 25.Qxh7 Qxf2+ 26.Kh1 Qxg2# you won with a nice mating finish.

review.turning_point: 18...Rc3! answered White's overreach and kept control after the complications.
review.focus: At 21...Re7 you moved a defender and almost lost. Before making a move that blocks the e-file or the back rank, check your opponent's checks first.

review.headline: An even endgame that was lost in time trouble

sections.text: As Black you answered the Queen's Gambit with the Exchange line of 2...e6 and set up solidly with 5...Bd6 and 6...O-O. After 11.Bxf6 Qxf6 and 15...Nf6 the game was very balanced.
A tactical moment came at 26.Rd1?, which allowed 26...Rxd1+! with a back rank idea: your rook took on d1 and after 27.Nxd1 the pieces were traded. The position remained roughly level.
Then the endgame went wrong. 33...a5?? was a blunder (the engine preferred 33...Kf7), but White returned the favour with 34.gxf5?? and you found the strong 34...axb4!. The game was balanced again.
Low on time, you played 35...Bd8 and 36...Be7??, and then 37...c5?? was the final blow: 37...cxb5 was the move. After 38.Nxe4 the e4 pawn fell, and 40.b6 and 41.Nxc5 ended resistance.

review.turning_point: 37...c5 turned a balanced endgame into a lost one (-0.2 to -5.5).
review.focus: Clock management in the endgame: 33...a5, 35...Bd8, 36...Be7 and 37...c5 all came in time trouble. Keep more time for the ending.

review.headline: A winning position from the opening that slipped away in time trouble

sections.text: You took the initiative against 3...h6 with 4.d4, and after 6.Qxd4 Qf6 7.Be3 Qxd4 8.Bxd4 you went into an ending with a pleasant lead in development. 10.O-O-O was natural.
Black helped with 10...c5?, and you found 11.Be3!. Later 14.Bxb7! picked up a pawn and you maintained pressure with 15.Bd5, 17.Bf4 and 18.Bxe5. By move 19 you were around +2.5.
You kept the lead with 21.Rhd1 and 26.Rdg2, reaching +3.8 at move 28. 29.gxf6?? was the first big slip, because 29.cxd5 was the right recapture. After 29...Bxe4 the evaluation moved to -1.9.

Low on time, you still had resources: 32.Re1! was good and 36.Re8! made good use of the pin on the eighth rank. But 33.Ree7??, 34.Rac7?? and 35.f7? each cost you something, and the clock ran out at 41 moves with the game almost level.

review.turning_point: 29.gxf6 gave up a clearly winning position (+3.8 to -1.8) because you did not recapture on d5.
review.focus: At 29.gxf6, recapture first. When your opponent takes a piece, as with 28...Bxd5, look at 29.cxd5 before going for your own plan.

review.headline: A clean attacking win ending in mate

sections.text: You played the Italian with 4.d4 and then followed up well with 5.Nxd4 Nxd4 6.Qxd4, putting your queen in the centre. 7.Nc3 and 8.e5 gained space.
9.exd6 was a small mistake (the engine preferred 9.e6), but you recovered with 10.Bf4 and 11.Bxd6. 12.O-O-O Qg5+ 13.Kb1 Qf5 14.Rhe1 prepared the next shot, and Black's 14...Nxf2 let you in.

15.Nd5 was a strong reply. Black erred with 15...Qg5, and 16.Qxf2! took the knight with a pin on the f-file, taking the evaluation to +5.0. After 17.Ne7+ Kh7 18.Qxf5+ queens came off with you far ahead.
From there you cleaned up carefully with 20.Nxd6, 21.Nxf7 and 22.Nxd8. 23.Re7+ Kg8 24.Ne6 Rf2 25.Rd8+ Rf8 26.Rxf8# was a fine finish.

review.turning_point: 16.Qxf2! took advantage of 15...Qg5 and moved the evaluation from +2.8 to +5.0.
review.focus: At 9.exd6 you gave up some of your edge; 9.e6 kept more pressure. Look for moves that keep the opponent cramped.

review.headline: A comfortable London opening that ended on the clock

sections.text: You met the Jobava-style set-up with the standard 2...e6, 3...Bd6 and 4...Bxf4 5.exf4. After 6.Nf3 O-O 7.h4 you were in an easy position with the bishop pair gone and a good structure.
7...c6 was slightly passive; 7...c5 was the move. White's 8.Ne5 and 9.g4 started a pawn storm, and 9...Nxe5 10.fxe5 was fine.
10...Ne8 was another inaccuracy (-1.5), because 10...Nd7 kept the knight active. After 11.g5 f6 12.exf6 gxf6 13.g6 White had a lot of space.
The result was a loss on time at move 13, with the evaluation at -1.3: clearly worse, but a very long way from lost. The clock decided the game, not the position.

review.turning_point: 10...Ne8 let White's pawn storm roll with 11.g5, moving the evaluation to around -1.5.
review.focus: At 10...Ne8 you retreated into a passive corner. Keep your pieces active against the pawn storm with 10...Nd7.

review.headline: A Sicilian where you drifted, then lost your queen with 13.Bxf6

sections.text: You played the Open Sicilian with 3.d4 and 5.Bc4, and Black's 7...d5? was a real mistake. You found 8.exd5!, which was the right answer.
Then you gave the advantage away. 6.Qf3, 7.Nb3, 9.Bb5, 10.Nc3 and 11.Bg5 each put pieces on awkward squares. By 11...Re8+ you were around -2.3.
13.Bxf6?? was the major blunder: after 13...Bxf3 you were down about six points. 13.Qxg4 was needed, because your queen was attacked and the bishop trade on f6 did not help.
Black returned the favour with 14...Bxe2, and you found 15.Nxe2!, but 16.Kd2 and 18.Nbd4 were the final slips. You resigned at move 18.

review.turning_point: 13.Bxf6 left your queen en prise (-1.3 to -3.8) when 13.Qxg4 was the right move.
review.focus: At 13.Bxf6, check every attacked piece before making your own capture. 13.Qxg4 removed the attacker first.

review.headline: A short Sicilian where 11.e5 hung a pawn and 12.Bg5 hung a bishop

sections.text: You played the open Sicilian with 3.d4 and 4.Nxd4, and the opening was solid. Black's 4...Bb4+ forced 5.c3 Bc5, and you developed with 6.Be3, 7.Bd3, 8.O-O and 9.Re1.

6.Be3 was slightly inaccurate, but nothing worrying. The first real error was 11.e5??. The pawn push felt natural after 10...d5, but it lost a pawn to 11...Nxe5 and cost you the centre. The engine preferred 11.Bg5.

12.Bg5?? was a blunder. It moved the bishop from e3, so your rook on e1 faced the knight on e5, a discovered attack. But your bishop on d3 was attacked by that same knight, and 12...Nxd3 simply took it.
The engine suggested 12.Bc2, saving the bishop. You resigned right away. A quick glance at the knight's captures would have saved the game.

review.turning_point: 12.Bg5 left the bishop on d3 hanging to the knight on e5 (-1.3 to -4.8).
review.focus: Check what your opponent can capture before every move: 12.Bg5 ignored the bishop on d3, and 12.Bc2 would have kept the game alive.

review.headline: A solid opening, a missed chance on move 12, then a rook hung on move 14

sections.text: A quiet Leonardis setup where you developed sensibly: 3...Nf6, 4...Be6, 5...Nbd7 and 6...Be7 gave you a sound position, and the engine only had White about a third of a pawn ahead. When White broke with 8.d4 you took the pawn with 8...exd4, and after 9.Nxd4 O-O 10.Nxe6 fxe6 the game was level and healthy.

White then pushed 11.f4 and 12.f5?, a mistake that loosened the center and moved you from -0.9 to +0.6. You had a good answer in 12...exf5, when 13.Qd2 fxe4 14.Nxe4 d5 keeps your structure healthy and your pieces active. Instead 12...Nc7? sent the knight away from the action and flipped the evaluation to -0.6.

After 13.fxe6 Nxe6 14.Bc4 you were only slightly worse, and there was a real chance at 14...Rxf1+, a back rank shot that would have won material. You played 14...Rf6?? instead, and 15.Rxf6 just took a rook. That ended the game.

review.turning_point: 14...Rf6?? walked into 15.Rxf6 and lost a rook when the checking capture 14...Rxf1+ was available.
review.focus: Before every move, list the checks and captures for both sides. At 14...Rf6 the capture 14...Rxf1+ was sitting on the board, and the rook you moved was hanging.

review.headline: An early pawn storm on your own kingside that cost pawns and then the clock

sections.text: White opened with the Levitsky Attack, 2.Bg5, and you answered with 2...f6. That is a fair way to challenge the bishop, and after 3.Bh4 you were still about level. The trouble began with 3...g5?, which loosened your king's cover for the rest of the game; the engine preferred 3...Nh6 followed by 4.f3.

After 4.Bg3 h5 5.h4 the h-file was wide open against you and you were already down about a full pawn in evaluation. Still, 6.e3 e5?! was an interesting counter, and White did not find the strongest answer: 7.Be2? was a mistake, and 7.hxg5 fxg5 8.Rxh5 was the sharper try.

You then played 7...Bd6?!, and 8.Bxh5+ won a pawn with check. 8...Kd7? walked the king into the middle, whereas 8...Kf8 was the engine choice. 9.hxg5 took a second pawn and 9...fxg5? made it worse; 9...Ke7 was the move.

At the end 10.Qg4+ was a check on the board and you ran out of time. By then the evaluation was around -4.5, so the position was already difficult, but the flag falling meant you never got to fight on.

review.turning_point: 3...g5? opened lines against your own king, and the later 8.Bxh5+ and 9.hxg5 took the pawns that structure could no longer protect.
review.focus: Be careful with kingside pawn pushes early on: 3...g5 gave White the h-file and the h5 pawn. Keep the structure and develop first, as in the engine's 3...Nh6.

review.headline: A calm Two Knights opening that was fully playable when the game ended

sections.text: This was a normal Italian game against the Two Knights Defense: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 and 4.O-O. Your accuracy was 90.8 with no errors, and every move you made was a sensible developing choice.

After 4.O-O Be7 the evaluation was roughly level, around +0.3 for you. White has the extra move, the pieces are developed, and Black has not created any weaknesses. There were no tactical problems in the position and no reason to give it up.

The record shows the game ended only four moves in, with a resignation. That is hard to justify from the position: nothing had gone wrong, and a level game against a similarly rated opponent is worth playing out.

review.turning_point: There was no turning point on the board. The position after 4...Be7 was level, so the result came from the decision to stop playing, not from anything that happened over the board.
review.focus: Keep playing in level positions. After 4.O-O Be7 you had a comfortable game, and a blitz game at this stage is far from decided.

review.headline: A well-played Italian where one slip on move 14 let Black take over the initiative, then you fought back to equality

sections.text: You played the Italian with Paris Defense confidently: 4.Nc3, 5.O-O and 6.d4 followed by 8.Qxd4 gave you the center and a small edge, around +0.5. 9.Be3 O-O was a natural continuation with an easy plan of putting your pieces on good squares.

The first inaccuracy was 10.e5?!, which opened the position and handed Black easy play: 10...dxe5 11.Qxe5 Bd6 12.Qd4 brought the queen back and the evaluation to about level. Then 12...Ng4 attacked your bishop, and 13.g3?! left the kingside a bit loose.

The real mistake was 14.h3?, which dropped you to -1.7. The engine preferred 14.Bf4 Ne5, just moving the bishop out of danger. After 14...Nxe3 15.fxe3 your structure was damaged, and you were worse until you fought back with 16.Rf3 and 17.Qd3.

The end is the best part of your game. After 18.Qxc4 Qg5, 19.Qxf7+ won a pawn, and 21.Nf6+! was the engine's best move, putting a piece en prise to keep things level. After 21...Kh8 the position was about 0.0, so resigning there was not necessary.

review.turning_point: 14.h3? let the knight take on e3 and left your pawns scattered and gave Black the better game, when 14.Bf4 would have kept things level.
review.focus: At 14.h3 your instinct was to ask the knight on g4 a question. Before that, check whether the knight can just capture a piece. Moving 14.Bf4 first would have avoided damaging your pawn structure.

review.headline: A winning position built in the middlegame, then thrown away in time trouble

sections.text: In this London System you traded on e5 with 9...Nxe5 10.dxe5 and kept the game equal. The first real chance came when White played 14.Bb5? and 15.Bxd7?, both errors, and you answered correctly with 15...Qxd7! to keep material even and take over the initiative.

You played 21...Qxc2 to win a pawn and 23...Qxb2 for a second, and after 25.Rc6? you found 25...b4!, a strong answer that opened lines against White's pieces. With 26.Rf2?? White made a serious error, and the position was +2.7 in your favor.

From there the clock hurt you. 26...b3? gave back a lot, 28...Rb4?? dropped the evaluation from +2.8 to 0.0, and 31...Rb4?? did the same again at +3.5. Engine lines such as 28...fxe5 or 31...Qa4, which would have forked the rook on c6 and bishop on d4, were there to find.
At the end 32...Ra8?? and 33...Rb5?? finished it. 33...Rb5 stepped off the diagonal and left the queen on a3 to be taken by 34.Bxa3, which cost you the queen.

review.turning_point: The advantage went with 28...Rb4??, a hurried move when you were clearly better. Every later move was played under pressure.
review.focus: Your technique got you to a winning position, but 28...Rb4 is where it slipped. With little time, choose simple, safe moves and keep your pieces protected.

review.headline: A comfortable Italian ruined by one hasty knight jump

sections.text: You played the Italian well. After 5.d4 exd4 6.Nxd4 Nxd4 7.Qxd4 d6 you had the center and the better position, about +0.8 on the engine, with 8.Bg5 and 9.Bh4 putting pressure on the knight on f6.

Black castled with 9...O-O and the position was still comfortable for you. The engine suggested 10.O-O-O Be6, bringing the king to safety and keeping the extra space. That would have kept a clean edge with no risk.
Instead 10.Nd5?? offered the knight where it could just be taken. After 10...Nxd5 you were down a piece and the evaluation dropped to -4.7, which is why you resigned.

review.turning_point: 10.Nd5?? is the moment: from +0.8 you fell to -4.6, losing a knight to 10...Nxd5.
review.focus: On 10.Nd5, ask whether the piece is protected and what can capture it. A knight jump that looks active needs to be checked against 10...Nxd5.

review.headline: A swingy Petrov where both sides traded blunders until the final king move

sections.text: In the Three Knights Petrov you traded smoothly: 6...exd4, 8...fxe6 and 10...Bxf6 kept you level, and 11.Bh5+ Ke7 was a safe answer. After 12.O-O Bxc3 13.bxc3 the position was roughly level.

13...Ne5?? was the first big error, dropping you to -2.2; the engine preferred 13...g5 14.Qe2. White returned the favor straight away with 14.Qd4?? and you were back to +0.6, but 14...Qf8?? let it slip again.

The game kept swinging. 17.Qd5?? gave you a chance and you had the stronger 17...Ng5; 17...c6?? threw it away. 18.Qa5?? was another gift and 18...Qd8! was a good answer. 19.Qb4 Qd7?? then missed 19...Qb6+.
The end came with 22.f6+. Capturing with 22...gxf6 was the engine move, but 22...Kd8?? went to -8.4, and 23.fxg7 finished it.

review.turning_point: 22...Kd8?? turned a difficult but playable position into a lost one, when 22...gxf6 was available.
review.focus: At 22...Kd8 you had a simple capture in 22...gxf6. When there's a check or capture available, calculate it first before moving the king.

review.headline: A comfortable Petrov that ended in a one-move mate

sections.text: You met the Petrov with 3...d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4, a sound sequence, and traded down with 9.Bxf6 Qxf6 10.Nxe6 fxe6. After 12.O-O-O O-O-O you were level and had a healthy position.
You then played steady moves, 15...e5, 16...a6, 17...g5 and 18...Bg7, and the engine had you a little ahead, around +1.0, with White's pieces tied up. This was a good, patient middlegame.
19.Qe4 was a strong move: it aimed at b7 with the bishop on g2 behind it. You needed to respond to that threat. 19...d5 20.Qb4 would have blocked the diagonal and kept your edge.
Instead 19...Rhe8?? ignored it, and 20.Qxb7# was mate. It was your only error, but it ended the game.

review.turning_point: 19...Rhe8?? missed the threat against b7, and 20.Qxb7# was checkmate.
review.focus: When the opponent's queen comes to a new square, ask what it attacks next. After 19.Qe4 the threat on b7 was the first thing to check, and 19...d5 would have stopped it.

review.headline: A wild King's Gambit where you were worse for most of the game but found a big swing before the end

sections.text: In the King's Gambit you took the pawn with 3...exf4, which was fine, but 2...d6?! and 4...c6? were slow. The engine preferred 4...g5, hitting back at once. After 5.Bxf4 Nf6 6.e5 dxe5 7.Nxe5 you were a little worse but solid.

White's 10.Bg5? was a mistake that gave you the chance to equalize. You continued with 10...O-O?! and traded on f6. After 14.Qg4+ Kh8 you were fine, but 15...Nd7?? lost the e6 pawn to 16.Qxe6 where 15...f5 would have held things together.

You then slid further, with 20...Bf4? and 22...Nf4?!. White set up a trick with 23.Ne5 and played 24.Nf7+?, a discovered attack on your bishop on d4 that looked strong but let you answer 24...Qxf7!, and you came out ahead on material.
25...Qg6? let White back in and 27.Qf6+?? gave you another chance, which you took with 27...Qxf6!. But 28...Rxg2?? lost a knight to 29.Rxf4, and 33.Rg8# ended the game.

review.turning_point: 28...Rxg2?? undid your comeback and cost a knight to 29.Rxf4, when 28...Rd8 was the safe move.
review.focus: 15...Nd7 gave away the e6 pawn and the initiative. When your king is exposed on h8, look at forcing moves like 15...f5 before retreating pieces.

review.headline: A brilliant attack that missed a mate and then missed it again

sections.text: This was a Two Knights Defense with 4.Ng5, and you played it very well. After 5.exd5 Nxd5? you found the right idea, 6.Nxf7!, a fork of the queen on d8 and the rook on h8. Then 7.Qf3+ drove the king to e6.
8...Nd4? was another mistake by Black, and you answered with 9.Bxd5+!, regaining the piece and keeping the attack. By 10.Qf7 you were up about +1.6, with Black's king stuck in the middle.

10...Nxc2+?? was a fork of your king and rook, but it was a blunder, and you were at +4.9. 11.Ke2?? gave that away, though; 11.Kd1 was safer. Then 11...Nxa1?? put you in a forced win, and you missed 12.Ne4#, a mate on the spot. 12.Nb5+?? played on instead.

More mistakes followed: 14.Nxa8?? and 19.Kd3?? gave up your advantage, and 21.Qh4?? was the final blunder, when 21.Qxb7+ kept things going. You found good moves with 18.gxf3! and 20.Ke2!, but the early lead had already been given up.

review.turning_point: 12.Nb5+?? passed up the immediate mate with 12.Ne4#, and the winning attack was gone.
review.focus: At 12.Nb5+ the opponent's king was exposed, and 12.Ne4# was mate. When attacking, list every check first: the best attacking moves are often the most forcing.

review.headline: You took over after a poor opening when White overreached, and finished with a mate

sections.text: A quiet Queen's Pawn game where 8.f4 gave White some space. Then 9.e4 hit the center, and 9...Bb7?? let White take over, dropping you to -3.7. The engine preferred 9...dxe4 10.Nxe4, trading in the center.

You held on with 10...Bb4, 11...Nxf6 and 13...O-O, and White's pressure grew until 15.Bxh6?? gave you the chance. Your answer 15...gxh6! was correct, and the evaluation went from -3.3 to roughly level.
17.Bxd5?? was a second White error, and again you found the right answer, 17...Nxd5!. After 18.Nxd5 Bxd5 you were clearly ahead, and 19...Bxb2 and 20...Bxc1 picked up more material.
You kept the queen active with 23...Qxf5 and 24...Qd5, then closed it with 29...Qh1+!, a skewer on the first rank with a back rank flavor. After 30.Kf2 Qg2# it was mate.

review.turning_point: 17.Bxd5?? and your answer 17...Nxd5! won material and left White with no good way back.
review.focus: 9...Bb7 allowed 10.e5 and let White take over. When the center is tense, resolve it first, as with 9...dxe4.

review.headline: A quick Italian win where Black blundered and you were still fine at the end

sections.text: You played a standard Italian with 4.c3 and 5.d4, the classical way to claim the center. After 5...exd4 6.cxd4 you were fine, and Black's 6...Bb6? was a mistake, since 6...Bb4+ was the better check.
7.O-O?! was slightly slow, but Black followed with 7...O-O?, leaving you at +2.0. Then 8.e5? gave some of that back, since the engine preferred 8.d5, gaining space and pushing the knight away.

Black played 8...Ne4??, which looks active but loses the initiative. You were at +3.5 and the best move was 9.Bd5, hitting the knights and the f7 pawn, pinning the f7 pawn. 9.Re1?? let Black off the hook, but the opponent resigned anyway.

review.turning_point: 8...Ne4?? gave you a winning edge, and 9.Re1?? gave most of it back. 9.Bd5 was the move to find.
review.focus: At 9.Re1 you had a strong forcing move in 9.Bd5. Ahead in the opening, look for the move that attacks the most pieces at once.

review.headline: You weathered an early storm and punished White's pawn push

sections.text: In the Bishop's Opening you traded bishops with 4.Bxe6 fxe6 and developed with 5...Nf6, 6...c6 and 7...Be7. White castled long with 8.O-O-O and began a pawn storm with 9.g4, which was dangerous.
9...Qa5? was a small error; the engine preferred 9...h6 10.h4. White pushed 10.g5 and 11.f4, and you castled queenside with 11...O-O-O, a decent counter.
12.f5?? was a big mistake, and you answered perfectly with 12...exf5!. Then 14.Qf2?? gave you the next chance, and 14...d4! forked the knight on c3 and bishop on e3. You came out ahead.
16...Ndf6? uncovered the rook on d8 against the queen, a discovered attack, but 16...Bxg5+ was stronger. You still came through, and 26...Rxf7 and 27...Rf1+ finished the job.

review.turning_point: 14...d4! forked the knight and bishop, and White could not hold both.
review.focus: 9...Qa5 spent time while White was building a pawn storm. A calmer move such as 9...h6 would have slowed the attack.

review.headline: A messy London game where you were lucky to survive an early blunder and won on time

sections.text: Against the London you traded well: 5...Ne4 6.Ne5 Nxg3 7.hxg3, then you played 7...f6??, which dropped you to -5.6. The engine preferred 7...Bxe5, the safer capture.
White missed the punishment: 8.Qh5+ was the shot, with the h7 pawn pinned against the rook on h8. 8.Nd3?? let you off, and 9...g6! was a good answer to 9.Qh5+?? after 8...e5?!.

11...f5?? gave White another chance, but 12.Nxd5? let you in again. You found 12...Bxg3!, which took a pawn with a discovered attack: the bishop leaving d6 opened the d-file for your queen against the knight on d5.
29...Bxa2?? was another error, but 30.Kxa2?? gave it back and you found 30...c6!. From there, 35...Nxa4! and the passed h-pawn won the game, and White ran out of time.

review.turning_point: 12...Bxg3! used a discovered attack to set up 13...Qxd5 and bring you back into the game.
review.focus: At 7...f6 you had 7...Bxe5, a simple capture. In the opening, check for captures that win material before making a pawn move.

review.headline: A Sicilian where one pawn capture left a knight hanging

sections.text: You played a standard open Sicilian with 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3, and after 5...e5 chose the active 6.Nf5?!. It was a bit double-edged: the knight on f5 looked strong but needed support, and 6...d5 hit the center.
7.exd5?? was the blunder. It took a pawn but left the knight on f5 to be captured by 7...Bxf5, and you were down a piece at -4.0. The engine preferred 7.Qf3 d4.
After that Black played accurately: 8...Bb4, 9...Qxf6 and 11...e4 kept the pressure on. 17.c5?! was a fork of the queen and bishop, but 17...Nxc5 just took the pawn.
Black kept control with 19...Rfe8 and 20...Re1+, and you resigned after 25.Kc2.

review.turning_point: 7.exd5?? grabbed a pawn but left the knight on f5 hanging, which decided the game.
review.focus: On 7.exd5, check what each of your pieces is protecting before capturing. The knight on f5 had no defender.

review.headline: A winning position built up over 45 moves, then lost in time trouble

sections.text: In the Philidor you played 4...Be7?! and White pushed 5.d5?, a mistake. You grabbed the pawn with 5...Nxe4, which the engine did not love; it preferred 5...c6. But White returned the favor with 6.c4??, when 6.Qa4+ would have forked the king and knight.
You then played steadily: 10...Nxd3, 15...Nxc4 and 18...Bxc3 kept the extra material. 20...Ne3? gave a little back, but 22.Rxe2?? helped you, and you reached +8.3 after 29...Bh3+.
Even at 45...f3 you were clearly winning. 46...f2+?? was the error: the engine found a forced mate starting with 46...Qd4+. After 46...f2+ 47.Kf1 the position was level.
Low on time, you played 48...Qf5?? and 49...Qf7??, and 54.a8=Q put White's a-pawn on the board as a queen. You resigned at move 57.

review.turning_point: 46...f2+?? threw away a forced mate when 46...Qd4+ was available.
review.focus: At 46...f2+ you were up a lot and the king was exposed. Look for the check first: 46...Qd4+ was the winning move, and the low clock made it harder.

review.headline: A good Scandinavian that turned on one hanging rook

sections.text: You handled the Scandinavian well: 2.exd5 Qxd5 3.Nc3, then 4.d4, 5.Nf3 and 7.Bg5 gave you the usual small edge, around +0.8. 11.Ne5 and 12.Bxe7 simplified into a good position.

14.Bg4?! was a little loose, and Black's 14...Nc6? let you back in. After 15.Bxf5 exf5, 16.Qxf5? was a mistake, since 16.d5 was the engine move. Black missed 16...Nxd4 and played 16...Nxe5??, which put you ahead.
19.Rd7?? was the blunder. The simple 19.Rxd8 kept the edge, but the rook on d7 was exposed, and Black answered 19...g6?? in a way that gave you 20.Qd3!, which kept you in the game.
21.g3?? left the rook on d7 en prise: 21...Qxd7 cost you heavy material, and the game ended soon after. 21.Nd5 would have kept things level.

review.turning_point: 19.Rd7?? put the rook on an exposed square when 19.Rxd8 was the simple move.
review.focus: At 19.Rd7 you went for the more ambitious move. Check that your rook has enough protection before putting it deep in the opponent's position.

review.headline: A French where you got ahead early, wobbled in the middle, and finished with a winning queen check

sections.text: The French opened normally, and Black's b5 and a5 plan got ambitious. 7.Bd3 Ba6 put you at +2.2, and 8.O-O? was a little careless, since 8.exd5 cxd5 9.Nxb5 was the engine move.
Black replied 9...axb4??, and you took full advantage with 10.Rxa6 and 11.Rxa8. After the trades with 11...Qxa8 12.Bxc3 you were clearly better, around +2.0.
18.Ne5? let Black back in, but 20...f5?? gave it away. You found 21.Qxc4!, winning a knight and pinning the e6 pawn to the king. 22.Qxc6?? was the mistake, since 22.Bxc6 kept the edge.
The game swung again, but 29...h6?? was Black's blunder. You found 30.Qe8+!, a fork of the king on h8 and the queen on b8 that was also a back rank check. 31.Qxb8 won the queen.

review.turning_point: 29...h6?? let you play 30.Qe8+!, forking the king and queen.
review.focus: 22.Qxc6 grabbed a pawn and gave away the advantage. When well ahead, choose the move that keeps pieces safe, like 22.Bxc6.

review.headline: An uneven Dragon where Black's one mistake rescued you

sections.text: In the Accelerated Dragon you went for 5.Bc4 and 6.c3, and Black replied with 6...Qb6. 7.Nb3?! and 8.Qd5?! were slow, and the position became about level, with Black a bit more comfortable.
After 9.Qb5 Bxc4 10.Qxc4 the queens were active, but Black's knights on e5 and b4 were starting to dominate. 15.Qc2?! and 16.Qb1? gave Black the upper hand at -3.6; the engine preferred 16.Qd1.
17.Re3?! made it worse, but Black played 17...Bh6??, which hit the rook but left the knight on d3 hanging. You found 18.Rxd3!, a clean answer, and after 18...Bxd2 19.Bxd2 you were a piece ahead.

review.turning_point: 17...Bh6?? left the knight on d3 hanging and 18.Rxd3! won a piece.
review.focus: 16.Qb1 let Black's knights take over the board. Keeping the queen on d1 would have kept the knights under control.

review.headline: A Colle where you gave back an edge, but White blundered more and you won in the end

sections.text: You played the Colle System well and traded with 8...Nxe5 9.dxe5 Nd7. 13...Bc5? was a mistake that dropped you to -1.2; the engine preferred 13...Qb6. White's 14.Rf3? gave you the chance to take over, and 15.Qe2 f5 was a decent plan.
16.b4?? and 19.Nxe4?? were big White mistakes. You replied 19...fxe4! and went to +4.0. Then 20.bxc5 exd3?? gave much of it back; the engine preferred 20...Qxb2 21.Qd1.
White's 21.cxb6?? gave you the move of the game: 21...dxe2! took the queen and put you clearly ahead. After 24.e4 Bxa3 and 26.Rxe2 Bxe2 you were winning, and the rooks and bishop did the rest.
The ending was a long technical task. You promoted with 48...h1=Q and finished with 56...Qc4#, a clean checkmate. Strong technique after the middle swings.

review.turning_point: 21...dxe2! took White's queen after 21.cxb6??, and the game was decided.
review.focus: At 20...exd3 you had the stronger 20...Qxb2. When you are winning, look for the capture that keeps the extra material, instead of a recapture that lets White back in.

review.headline: A free piece on move 4 won the game twice over, but you nearly gave it back in a wild middlegame

sections.text: This Philidor became a rout almost at once. After 3...Be6 your opponent played 4.O-O??, leaving the bishop on c4 to be taken, and you found 4...Bxc4 to win a clean piece. From there you were around +4 for most of the opening.

You then played the sensible plan of a player who is ahead: 8...Be7, 9...Qc8, and a kingside advance with 11...g5 and 12...g4 to get your queen into play. After 15.exf5 Qxf5 you were comfortably up material and the evaluation sat near +5.

The first wobble was 19...Ng4, which dropped you to +2.9, and 21...Ng4 repeated the idea. The bigger one came at 32...Nc6. Your opponent had just blundered with 32.Qd5+ (you were at +9.0), but 32...Nc6 swung the evaluation to -5.6 where 32...Qxd5 kept everything. Luckily 33.b4 gave it straight back and you found 33...Qxd5.

More slips followed: 38...Re8 gave away most of your edge where 38...Qxb4+ kept control, and 40...Kb6 allowed a forced mate. Your opponent missed it with 41.Nc6, and 41...Qxe3+ put you back in charge. You then promoted pawns and finished with 81...Kc2#.

review.turning_point: 32...Nc6 threw away a +9.0 position, and only 33.b4 followed by your 33...Qxd5 put you back on top.
review.focus: When you are far ahead, check every forcing capture before a quiet move. At 32...Nc6 the simple 32...Qxd5 kept the win, and at 40...Kb6 the safer 40...Kc8 avoided the forced mate.

review.headline: Clean Italian play, then a tactical shot punished a careless knight capture

sections.text: You played a calm, well-structured Italian. After 3...h6 you chose 4.d3 and 5.Qe2, and after 6.Be3 Bxe3 7.fxe3 you got an open f-file and a solid centre. Moves like 8.c3, 9.Bb3 and 10.Nbd2 built the position without any risk, which is why your accuracy was so high.
11.Bxe6 fxe6 12.d4 then went for the centre, and after 13.dxe5 dxe5 14.Nxe5 you had won a pawn. Your opponent answered with 14...Nh7?, which loosened their grip; 14...Nd7 was the engine's try.

You castled long with 15.O-O-O and kept adding pressure with 16.Ndc4. Then your opponent played 16...Nxc4??, the real blunder. You were ready with 17.Rxd8+!, a fork of the king on g8 and the rook on a8 that also worked as a back rank shot, since the king had no flight squares. After 17...Rxd8 you had traded a rook for their queen, and 18.Qxc4 collected the knight too.
Once up that much, you simplified with 19.Rf1 Rxf1+ 20.Qxf1 and your opponent resigned.

review.turning_point: 17.Rxd8+! right after 16...Nxc4?? turned a small edge into a decisive lead.
review.focus: You played nearly perfectly, so the lesson is to keep asking what your opponent's last move left undefended. That habit is what found 17.Rxd8+, and it is worth practising on quiet moments like 14.Nxe5 too.

review.headline: You were the one pressing in this Vienna, until 26...g6 and 27...Kh7 gave it all away

sections.text: A balanced opening. You answered 4.d3 with 4...Be6, took the trades after 5.Bxe6 fxe6 and 6.f4 exf4, and kept things level through 10.Bxf6 Bxf6 and 13.Nxf6+ Rxf6. Nothing in the first dozen moves worried you.

15...Nb6?! and 18...Qc7?! were slightly passive, and after 19.d4 exd4 20.Nxd4 you were still fine at +0.7. Then your opponent drifted with 21.Qg3?, and you took the chance to trade rooks with 21...Rxf1+ 22.Rxf1 Rxf1+ 23.Kxf1 Nxc4, winning a pawn.

24.b3? was another slip by White, and after 24...Ne5 25.Nf5 Qf7 26.Ke2 you stood about +1.2 with an extra pawn. The decisive error was 26...g6??, which sent the evaluation from +1.2 to -5.6. The engine preferred the calm 26...Qf6.

Your opponent then returned the favour with 27.Nxh6??, which put you back at +0.9, but 27...Kh7?? threw it away again. The engine's 27...Qe6 was the move, and after 27...Kh7 you were lost and resigned.

review.turning_point: 26...g6 turned a pawn-up position into a lost one, and 27...Kh7 missed the chance to repair it after 27.Nxh6.
review.focus: At 26...g6 you were better and only needed a safe move. Before a pawn push in front of your king, ask what it weakens, and compare it with a quiet queen move like 26...Qf6.

review.headline: A Scotch where the early queen trade went fine, but 11.Bd3 started the slide

sections.text: You chose the Scotch and handled the opening well: 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nxc6 dxc6 6.Qxd8+ Kxd8 forced the queens off at once, left Black with doubled c-pawns and a king stuck on d8, and you stood slightly better at +0.5.

7.e5?! pushed the pawn forward, and after 7...Ng4 8.Bg5+ Be7 9.Bxe7+ Kxe7 10.f4 Bf5 Black's pieces were active and your development lagged. The position had drifted to about even-to-slightly-worse for you (-0.7).

The decisive mistake was 11.Bd3?. It allowed 11...Bxd3 12.cxd3, which damaged your pawns, and 12...Ne3 put a knight on a strong square. The engine suggested 11.Ke2. After 13.Na3?! Nxg2+ and 14.Kf2?! Nxf4 you were two pawns down and Black's pieces were all active.
From there it was a long defence. You tried 16.Ke3 and 17.Ke4 with your king, but 18.exf6+ Nxf6+ only kept things going. 23.d4?! at the end gave away more, and you resigned after 23...Nf2.

review.turning_point: 11.Bd3 allowed a trade that wrecked your pawn structure and let the knight into e3.
review.focus: Look at 11.Bd3: before a developing move that lets the opponent trade and double your pawns, check what the recapture does to your structure. 11.Ke2 was less natural but avoided the damage.

review.headline: A sound QGD, then you let a gift slip when a safe line was available at 19...Qd5

sections.text: You met 1.d4 with a standard Queen's Gambit Declined set-up: 2...e6, 3...exd5 and 4...c6, then 5...Bd6 and 7...O-O. The opening was equal, and 9...Ne4 10.Nxe4 dxe4 gave you a typical pawn on e4 to work with.
11...Bf5?! and 12...Bg6?! were slightly loose, and by 14.Bxd6 Qxd6 15.Nc4 you were a little worse. 16...Qg5?! then invited 17.Bh3, and you answered with the active 17...Bh5.

Your opponent's 18.Rdf1? was a mistake and 19.f4?? was a real blunder, putting you at +2.3. The engine wanted 19...Qd5 to keep everything protected. Instead 19...Qh4?? handed the advantage back at -1.2.
20.Nd6 was strong, and 20...Bxf1?? allowed a forced mate. 20...Rf8 was needed. After 21.Qxf7+ you resigned.

review.turning_point: 19.f4?? gave you a clear advantage, but 19...Qh4?? let it slip and 20...Bxf1 finished it.
review.focus: When your opponent blunders, slow down. At 19...Qd5 the engine kept your extra edge and king safety, while 19...Qh4 left your own king exposed. Check every check and capture against your king before grabbing anything.

review.headline: A gambit won on a tactical sequence, then a long king-and-pawn finish

sections.text: Your opponent played the Danish Gambit and you accepted with 2...exd4 and 3...dxc3, going up material. Both sides played loosely: 4...Nc6?! and 5.Qd5?? from White gave you a chance to take control. Then 6...Nh6? let 7.Bxh6 gxh6 damage your structure, where 6...Bb4 was better.

After 9.O-O-O Be6?! and 10.Qd3 Nb4?! you were finding your feet. Your opponent then played 12.e5??, and you punished it with 12...Qf4+!, a check that also took aim at the loose bishop. After 13.Kb1 Qxc4 14.Qxc4 Bxc4 you were up material.
You nearly spoiled it with 20...Bc5??, which cut a +5.7 edge down to +0.1. The engine suggested 20...Bxh2. A series of trades followed and you reached a pawn ending.

That ending was tricky. 29...Kb4? gave up some of your advantage, but White replied 30.Kd4??, and your 30...Kxa4! was the move. You then ran your a-pawn home with 35...a1=Q+ and later picked off the last pawn with 39...Qxb6.

review.turning_point: 12.e5?? followed by your 12...Qf4+! won material and gave you the edge you needed.
review.focus: At 20...Bc5 you were winning and only needed to avoid letting your opponent off. The engine's 20...Bxh2 kept your edge, so check for the most forcing option before a quiet bishop move.

review.headline: A quick attacking win built on a bishop sacrifice at h6

sections.text: Your opponent's 2...a5 was an unusual move in this Caro-Kann, and you answered with 3.d4. After 4.Nc3?! dxe4 5.Nxe4 Nf6 the engine would have preferred 4.exd5 cxd5 5.Nc3, but you were still fine.
You developed naturally with 6.Bd3 and 8.O-O, and after 6...Nxe4 7.Bxe4 your bishop on e4 was aimed straight at the h7 square. After 10.h3 Bxf3 11.Qxf3, your queen joined in as well.
12.Qh5 h6 set up the key idea. 13.Bxh6! gxh6 14.Qxh6 gave up a bishop for two pawns, but it tore open the king's cover. The only defence was 14...f5, and your opponent instead played 14...Ra7??
15.Qh7# finished it. The queen on h7 was supported by the bishop on e4, so the king on g8 had nowhere to go. A very smooth attack.

review.turning_point: 13.Bxh6! opened the king and 14...Ra7?? missed the only defence, 14...f5.
review.focus: Your only slip was 4.Nc3?!. When Black takes space with 3...d5 like this, 4.exd5 cxd5 5.Nc3 keeps more pressure, so it is worth remembering for next time.

review.headline: A quiet French Exchange where early bishop moves cost a pawn, though you resigned in a playable position

sections.text: You played the Exchange French with 2.d4 and 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3. The queen chase went 4...Qa5 5.Bd2 Qb6 6.Nf3 Nf6, and you were comfortable, around +1.2.

7.Bb5+?! began to drift. After 7...c6 you retreated with 8.Ba4?!, which pinned the c6 pawn to the king but wasted time. The engine preferred 7.Bc4 and then 8.Bd3, keeping the bishop where it helped your development.

Black took the pawn with 8...Qxb2, and after 9.Bb3 Qa3 10.O-O Qd6 the engine still had you slightly ahead at +0.9 despite the missing pawn. 11.Bg5, 12.Re1 and 13.Qd2 were all sensible developing moves.
14.Ne5?! was the last slip, dropping the evaluation to -0.6, but that is far from lost. You resigned in a position that had plenty of play left.

review.turning_point: 7.Bb5+ and 8.Ba4 spent two moves on the bishop and let Black grab the b-pawn with 8...Qxb2.
review.focus: Against an early queen sortie, keep developing without moving the same piece twice. After 7.Bb5+ the engine liked 7.Bc4, so ask whether a check actually helps before you play it.

review.headline: You were doing well in the opening, then 10...O-O-O left a bishop hanging

sections.text: Your opponent chose an unusual set-up with 2.d3 and 3.g3, then played 4.Bh3?, which you answered correctly with 4...Bxh3 to trade bishops. After 5.Nxh3 Qd7 you were fine.
You developed with 6...Nc6, 7...d5 and 8...Bc5, and the engine had you better, around +1. Then 9...dxe4?! after 9.f3 opened the position before you were fully developed.

The decisive blunder came right away. After 10.Nxe4 you castled long with 10...O-O-O??, which left the bishop on c5 undefended, and 11.Nxc5 won it. The engine's 10...Bb6 would have kept the bishop safe and your edge intact.
You fought on with 15...Qh4?!, but after 17.Nxf7, 18.Nxh8 and 23.Bxe7 you were well behind in material and resigned after 24.Qxf3.

review.turning_point: 10...O-O-O left the c5 bishop hanging, and 11.Nxc5 won a piece.
review.focus: Before castling, check whether every piece is defended. At 10...O-O-O your bishop on c5 had no support, and a quick safety check would have led you to 10...Bb6.

review.headline: You won material early, then the flashy 16.Bd6 undid it

sections.text: This Philidor opened with 3.Bc4 Bg4 4.Nc3 c6 5.h3 Bh5 6.g4 Bg6 and 7.d4, a sharp set-up. After 8.dxe5 dxe5 9.Bg5 h6 10.Bh4 Be7 11.Bg3 you were fine.

Black then blundered with 11...Bb4??, and you found 12.Nxe5!. After 12...Qe7 13.Nxg6 fxg6 you were up material and the evaluation was about +3.7. 14.Qf3 and 15.O-O-O were natural, keeping everything protected.

Then came the key error. 16.Bd6?? looked like a fork of the bishop on b4 and the queen on e7, but 16...Bxd6 simply captured it and you were suddenly -4.1. The engine wanted 16.e5, which kept the pressure.

After that Black made mistakes of their own, including 18...a5?? and 19...b5??, but you gave the chances away. 19.Bb3?? missed 19.f4, and 25.e5?? and 27.Qe5?? kept dropping the evaluation. You resigned after 34.Qe5?!.

review.turning_point: 16.Bd6?? went for a fork that did not work, because 16...Bxd6 took the bishop.
review.focus: Before a flashy tactic like 16.Bd6, check whether the attacking piece can simply be taken. When you are winning, look for the quiet strong move, like 16.e5.

review.headline: A winning attack in the Scandinavian was thrown away when you grabbed on g7

sections.text: You met the Scandinavian well. After 2.exd5 Qxd5 3.Nc3 Qe5+ 4.Nge2 Bg4 5.d4 Bxe2 6.Bxe2 you had a lead in development, and your opponent's 7...Nd7? only helped you.

10.b3?? was a slip that took the sting out of the position, and your opponent returned the favour with 10...O-O-O??. You kept going with 12.Ng5 and 13.Bc4, and after 13...Be7? you struck with 14.Nxe6!, one of the best moves of the game.
16.Rxe7 and 17.Bxg8 then won a large amount of material, with the evaluation around +4. Your opponent's 17...Qxh2+ brought your king out to f1, though, and from here you had to be careful.

19.d5?? let the advantage slide, and 21.Rxg7?? was the final mistake. It allowed a forced mate. The engine's 21.Qg1 kept everything safe. After 22...Nge5+ you found 23.Bxe5, but 26.Qh5? lost to 28...Qxb4#.

review.turning_point: 21.Rxg7?? grabbed a pawn and let your opponent start a forced mating attack.
review.focus: When your king has been dragged out, as it was after 17...Qxh2+, check each queen check before grabbing material. At 21.Rxg7 the safe 21.Qg1 kept your lead.

review.headline: A chaotic game of missed mates on both sides, decided by the clock

sections.text: You answered the London with 2...e6 and 3...Bd6, then traded it off with 4...Bxf4 5.exf4, followed by 5...Nf6, 6...Nbd7 and 7...c5. 9...Nxd3 10.Qxd3 traded your knight for their bishop, and by 16.Qc3 you were roughly level.
Your opponent's 19.b3?? was a mistake and gave you a clear edge, but 19...Be2?? returned it. The engine suggested 19...Nf4. After 20.Nd7 both kings were under fire.

Then both sides missed forced mates. Your opponent's 21.Rxe2?? missed 21.Qxf8#, a back rank mate, and 22.Nxf8?? missed 22.Qxf8#. At 22...e5?? you missed 22...Qxa1+ with a forced mate, so there were several chances on both sides.
Later you had more slips: 23...e4?? where 23...Qc8 was better, and 24...Qf6?? where 24...Rxf2 was needed. You fought back with 25...h6! and 27...Kh7!, but 29...Qb2?? left you worse. You won on time.

review.turning_point: 19...Be2?? turned a good position into one where both sides could miss mates, and 22...e5?? missed the clearest one.
review.focus: At 22...e5 a forced mate with 22...Qxa1+ was available. When the kings are exposed, look at every check first. That habit would have saved you from several of these moves.

review.headline: A smooth Italian win that took off after a discovered attack with 18.d4

sections.text: A calm Giuoco Pianissimo with 4.d3 and 5.Be3 Bxe3 6.fxe3 gave you a solid centre. 7.O-O and 8.Qe2 were simple developing moves, and 9.Nc3 Be6 10.Bb3 Bxb3 11.axb3 kept the position healthy.
12.Nd5 Nxd5 13.exd5 Nb4 14.e4 gave you a strong pawn centre and space. Black played 14...a5 15.c3 Na6, and you won a pawn with 16.Rxa5, which was well timed.

Your opponent's 17...Qd7?? was the blunder, and you found 18.d4!, a discovered attack: moving the pawn from d3 opened the diagonal from your queen on e2 to the knight on a6. After 19.dxe5 dxe5 20.Rxa6 Rxa6 21.Qxa6 you were well ahead.

25...Rxd5? helped you further. 27.Qxb6?! was a small inaccuracy, since 27.Qb8+ first was cleaner, but the endgame after 30.Nxe5 was easily winning. You pushed the b-pawn with 36.b4, 37.b5 and 38.b6 and finished with 39.gxf4 and 40.fxg5.

review.turning_point: 18.d4! used a discovered attack on the knight on a6 right after 17...Qd7?? and won material by force.
review.focus: Your only inaccuracy was 27.Qxb6?!. When well ahead, play the extra check that improves your position first, as with 27.Qb8+, before taking the pawn.

review.headline: A messy French where your opponent's errors outweighed yours, finished on the clock

sections.text: You played 2...e6?! against 2.e4 and went for a Winawer set-up with 3...Bb4 4.a3 Bxc3+ 5.bxc3, which doubled White's pawns. 5...Nc6?! and 6...Bd7?! were not ideal, but your opponent's 6.Bb5? helped.
8...f6?? was an error, because 8...dxe4 was better. You followed with 9...e5? and 11...Qd6?, but your opponent kept finding mistakes like 9.Be3? and 12.f5??, so the game stayed close.

You grabbed a pawn with 14...Qxa3?!, but 15.Qd2?? and your 16...a5?? kept the position messy. Then 18.f6?? gave you the chance: you found 18...gxf6!, and after 19.Rxf6 O-O-O 20.Ng3 Bxf1 you were well ahead.
From there you were winning at about +8, with the extra material telling. The game ended when your opponent ran out of time after 25...Rd1.

review.turning_point: 18.f6?? followed by your 18...gxf6! turned a murky game into a clearly winning one.
review.focus: At 8...f6 you made a weakening pawn move. The engine suggested 8...dxe4, which relieved the centre. When the opening gets sharp, pick the simpler capture.

review.headline: You built a big material edge with strong play, then lost your queen on one careless capture

sections.text: Your opponent opened with 3...b6?, and you responded with 4.d4 exd4 5.Nxd4?!. 6.Qf3? and 7.Be3?? were inaccurate, and the engine liked 7.Nxc6 instead. Black answered with 7...Nxd4?? and 8...Bxe4??, which gave you the advantage back.
You found the right replies: 8.Bxd4! and 10.Bb5+!. After 9.Qe3?? d5?? the fight continued, and with 12.fxe4 and 14.exd5 you were clearly better.
You kept developing with 15.O-O, 16.Qg3 and 17.Qg4, and after 18.Bxe5 fxe5 19.Qe6+ Kh8 20.Bxe8 Qxe8 you were up a lot, around +5.8. Everything was under control.

Then came 21.Qxe5??. It looked like a pin on the bishop on e7 against the queen on e8, but 21...Bc5+ gave check and left your queen facing theirs, and 22...Qxe5 cost you the queen. The engine's 21.Nc3 was calm and safe. You resisted until move 44, but the game was lost.

review.turning_point: 21.Qxe5?? lost your queen after 21...Bc5+, turning +5.8 into -4.7.
review.focus: At 21.Qxe5 you were winning and needed only safe moves. Before capturing, check what your opponent can do with a check, as with 21...Bc5+. The calm 21.Nc3 kept the win.

review.headline: A messy but successful Two Knights win, helped by good tactics early and a long endgame

sections.text: You went for the Two Knights Italian with 4.O-O Bc5 5.d3 d5 6.exd5 Nxd5 7.Re1 O-O and took on e5 with 8.Nxe5 Nxe5 9.Rxe5. You were slightly better after 10.Qf3 and 11.Nd2, and then 12.Qg3?! drifted a little.

Black played 12...Bxf2+??, which looked like a fork of the king and queen, but 13.Kxf2! simply took the bishop. 14.Ne4?? was your error, but 14...Nxe4+?? let you off, and 15.Rxe4! won material. After 15...Qxg3+ 16.hxg3 you were well ahead.

In the endgame you had a big edge, but 31.Kxg4?? threw most of it away where 31.Rxg4 was cleaner, and 34.b4?? lost more. Black's 33...Kh5?? and 35...cxb5?? returned the favour, and your 36.axb5! was the right reply.
42.Kb7? was a mistake, but 43.c8=Q! got the pawn through. A few moves later you queened with 49.e8=Q and won.

review.turning_point: 14...Nxe4+?? let you off after your own 14.Ne4??, and 15.Rxe4! kept the edge.
review.focus: At 31.Kxg4 you were winning, and the engine's 31.Rxg4 would have kept it that way. In endgames, check for opponent pawn breaks like 31...f5+ before you move the king.

review.headline: A Scotch where Black blundered early and you won on time after missing a forced mate

sections.text: You played the Scotch with 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Nxd4 5.Qxd4 b6, then 6.Bc4?! and 7.Nd2?!, which were slightly loose. Black's 7...Bc5? and 8...Be7?? let you in: after 8.Qe5+ your queen pinned the bishop on e7 against the king (8...Be7), and you were at +5.5.
9.Qf4?? threw away that advantage, since the engine wanted 9.Qxg7. The middlegame stayed balanced, with 14.Qg3?! and 15.Qg5 offering a queen trade that you did not need.

You kept finding good moves, including 17.O-O! and 27.Rxd3!. 31.Rd8 was a pin on the rook on f8, but it was a blunder, and 31...Rxd8?? let you back in. 32.Rxd8+! was a back rank idea that regained the initiative.
You missed a forced win twice: 34.Bf4?? and 35.Bg5?? both overlooked 34.Bh6, which ran 34.Bh6 Rf2+ 35.Kxf2 c4 36.Rxf8#. Finally 36.Bh6! was right, and you won on time.

review.turning_point: 32.Rxd8+! brought you back from a bad moment, and 36.Bh6! showed the winning idea.
review.focus: At 34.Bf4 and 35.Bg5 you missed the forced mate starting with 34.Bh6. When the opponent's king is boxed in, look for checks before quiet moves.

review.headline: A shaky Petrov that you turned around with a queen check and a swindle

sections.text: You played 3...Bc5?? against 3.Bc4, which left you slightly worse where 3...Nxe4 was safer. Fortunately 4.O-O? and 5.d3 gave you time, and you got your king castled with 5...O-O.
6.Bg5 Be6 7.Bb3 h6 8.Bh4 Nbd7 9.c3 d5?! was a bit loose, and after 10.Bxf6 Nxf6 11.Nxe5 dxe4 you were fine. 13.f4? by your opponent gave you a chance.
13...Bxe5?? was a blunder, since 13...Bxb3 was better. Later 15...Qg5?, 16...Ne3? and 17...Nf5?? kept you on the back foot, and your opponent had the edge.
Then White played 18.Rg4?? and you found 18...Qc1+!, a back rank check. After 19.Qf1 Qxf1+ 20.Kxf1 Ne3+ 21.Kf2 Nxg4+ you had won the rook and the game.

review.turning_point: 18.Rg4?? allowed 18...Qc1+!, which forced the queen trade and won the rook.
review.focus: At 13...Bxe5 you gave up the chance to win a piece. The engine's 13...Bxb3 kept the position safe. Before recapturing, look at whether a bigger capture is available.

review.headline: A short, sharp Two Knights win built on the discovered attack 9.Nxe7+

sections.text: You played the Two Knights with 4.O-O Bc5 5.d3 d6, then developed calmly with 6.Be3 and 7.Nc3. Your accuracy was very high.
8.Nd5 was the key idea. It attacked the queen on e7 and set up a threat against the bishop on e6. Black replied 8...O-O-O??, missing the engine's 8...Qd8.

You found 9.Nxe7+!, a discovered attack: the knight moved with check and uncovered your bishop on c4 against the bishop on e6. After 9...Nxe7 10.Bxe6+ fxe6 11.Bxc5 dxc5 you had won a queen for a knight.
12.Ng5 and 13.Nxe6 finished the job, and Black resigned.

review.turning_point: 9.Nxe7+! won the queen for a knight right after 8...O-O-O??.
review.focus: You played cleanly, so keep working on the same habit: look at where your opponent's pieces are loose, as with the queen and bishop on e7 and e6 before 8.Nd5.

review.headline: A Petrov where 10...Qe7 cost a rook, and mates were missed on both sides

sections.text: Your opponent played an Italian-style set-up with 4.Bc4, 5.Bd5 and 6.Bxe6 fxe6. After 7.h3 Nbd7 8.d4 exd4 9.Nxd4, your 9...e5? was the first mistake, and the engine wanted 9...Nc5 here.
10.Ne6 was a strong jump, and 10...Qe7?? made it worse. The engine suggested 10...Qa5. After 11.Nc7+ Kf7 12.Nxa8 you were down a lot of material.
You fought back well: 14...Qxf6, then 15...Be7, a discovered attack that opened the h8 rook against the knight on a8. After 16.O-O? Rxa8! you got the knight back and the position was closer.

17...Qh4? and 21...Rd8?! lost ground, and 22...Rd2?? allowed a forced mate. Your opponent also missed one with 26.Rf7??, when 26.Qf7+ finished it. Finally 27...Nf4? allowed another forced mate and 28.Rxf4+ ended the game.

review.turning_point: 10...Qe7?? allowed 11.Nc7+ and 12.Nxa8, which cost you a rook.
review.focus: At 22...Rd2 you were still in the game and the engine wanted 22...b5. When you are down material, check your own king before making a threat, since that move allowed a forced mate.

review.headline: A Stafford Gambit you handled well early, lost control of, then rescued with a final tactic

sections.text: Black went for the Stafford Gambit and you took the pawn with 3.Nxe5. After 3...Nc6? (3...d6 was the safer move) you found the right idea in 4.Nxc6, which wrecked Black's pawn structure after 4...dxc6. For a long stretch you were comfortably better, around +2.

The advantage started to leak with 10.e5?! and then vanished at 15.Be3??, which swung the evaluation from +1.3 to -1.2. Black returned the favour with 15...g5??, when 15...Nxe3 16.fxe3 was stronger. You then followed with 16.c4??; 16.exf6 was the move, and after 16...Nxe3 17.fxe3 Black's kingside pawns took over.

You were around -2.7 for most of the middlegame, but 23...b5?? after your 23.c5 handed you a lifeline, and the evaluation jumped to +3.9. You let it slip again with 24.Qa5??, and 24...exd4 kept Black in the game.
The finish came from a calm move: 25.Nb4!, and after 26.Qa6+ Kb8 you played 27.Nxc6+, which forked the king and queen and ended the game.

review.turning_point: 27.Nxc6+ forked king and queen after Black walked into it with 26...Kb8; the swing started with 23...b5, which gave you back a position you had thrown away.
review.focus: At 16.c4 you could have taken 16.exf6 and kept the edge. When the opponent has pawn pushes like ...g5 available, check them before you play a quiet move such as 15.Be3.

review.headline: A queenside pawn-break that paid off, a tangle in the middle, and a mate delivered despite a late slip

sections.text: This began as a slow Queen's Pawn game where White pushed on the queenside with 4.c4, 5.c5 and 8.b4. You answered the loose 9.Bd2?? with 9...axb4!, opening the a-file, and after 10.Bxb4 bxc5 11.dxc5 you were already ahead.

You lost the thread briefly with 13...e5??, which flipped the evaluation from +2.6 to -2.6 after 14.Nxc6; 13...Bd7 was the safer move. You still found tactics. 15...Nb3 forked the rook on a1 and the queen on d2, and when White replied 16.Qd3?? you took 16...Nxa1!.

The next few moves were a whirlwind. 17...Nc2?? gave a lot back, but White answered with 18.Rc1??, and 18...Nxb4! started a run of captures that left you well ahead, with 22...Kxe7! cleaning up. By the time of 24.Nxd5+ you were clearly better.
Time pressure showed late. 26...Rxa3 and 34...f4 let the engine score drop, and 45...Kd6?? threw away a large lead. White returned the favour with 46.Nb3??, and 46...g3# ended it.

review.turning_point: 13...e5?? turned a good position into a bad one, and 15...Nb3 (the fork) followed by 16...Nxa1 brought you right back and decided the middlegame.
review.focus: 13...e5 opened the centre when you were not ready. 13...Bd7 kept everything protected. In a position where your king is still in the middle, ask what the opponent's pieces can reach before you open lines.

review.headline: A Queen's Gambit Declined where early awkwardness turned into a crushing attack

sections.text: After 3.Bf4 Bd6 White traded bishops with 4.Bxd6, and you recaptured with 4...cxd6?. The engine preferred 4...Qxd6, which would have kept your structure healthier. It did not hurt much, and you stayed solid with 6...Be6 and 7...Nc6.

White's 8.Qe3? put the queen in a pin-prone spot, and 8...a6? did not take advantage of it (8...Qb6 was stronger). White then took a pawn with 9.Nxd5, and you hit back with 9...Qa5+, a fork of the king on e1 and the knight on d5, though it was only worth +1.0 against the best play.

The game turned with 11.O-O-O??, which castled into trouble. 11...Rc8! pinned the knight on c3 to the king on c1, and after 12.Nf3 Nxa2+ the knight check also uncovered an attack from your queen on a5. 13.Kb1 Nxc3+ and you were a clear piece up, then more.
After that you simply kept the pressure on: 15...Nxe3, 18...Qxb2 and a long run of checks. Then 34...Bc2# finished the game.

review.turning_point: 11.O-O-O?? walked the king into 11...Rc8!, and the follow-up 12...Nxa2+ meant White never recovered.
review.focus: At 4...cxd6 the queen recapture 4...Qxd6 was better. When a bishop trade lands on d6, think about which recapture keeps your pawn structure and your development.

review.headline: A level game ended in one move when a bishop step left your queen hanging

sections.text: This was a Nimzowitsch-style opening where you took the pawn with 3.dxe5 and the position stayed fairly equal. Your 5.Bf4?! allowed 5...Nxf3+ 6.Qxf3 and Black developed easily with 6...Qe7.

You kept things going with 7.Bc4?! and 8.O-O?!, small slips that cost a few tenths. After 9.Re1 Bxf4 10.Qxf4 d6 11.Nc3 Be6 12.Nd5 Bxd5 13.exd5 you reached a level game with a queen each and active rooks, around -0.0.

Black's 14...Qa4 was a good move, hitting your bishop on c4 and pointing at the queen on f4. Here 15.Bb3?? lost on the spot. The bishop moved off the diagonal, which opened an attack from the queen on a4 against your queen on f4, and 15...Qxf4 took it for nothing. The engine suggested 15.Qd4 instead, keeping the queens safe.
The game was over immediately after that, and you resigned.

review.turning_point: 15.Bb3?? uncovered Black's queen on your queen, and 15...Qxf4 cost you nine points of material.
review.focus: Before every move, check what the move uncovers. At 15.Bb3 you moved the bishop away and left the queen on f4 undefended in the line of Black's queen; 15.Qd4 was the safe choice.

review.headline: A Hyperaccelerated Dragon where you drifted into a lost position, then got a gift in the rook ending

sections.text: You met the Dragon setup with 5.Bc4 and 6.O-O, but 8.Qf3?! let Black's knight jump to e5 with tempo, and 10.Bg5?! led to 10...Nxc4 11.Bxf6 Bxf6 12.Qxc4. The game was roughly level then but you were a little worse.
14.N2f3? and 15.Rad1?! were slow, and 20.Nd4?? gave away the advantage, but Black replied 20...Bd7??, missing 20...e5. You then found 21.Nd5!, the best move, and you were back in the game.
The big mistake was 24.Qd5??, which left your knight on b6 hanging; 24...Qxb6 cost you a piece. 24.a4 was the move. You were down about -5.6 and stayed down through 27.Qb3 Qxb3 28.axb3 Bxd4+ 29.Rxd4.

But the rook ending turned around. Black grabbed a pawn with 36...Rxc3??, and 37.bxc3! uncovered your rook on d2 against the rook on a2. After 37...Rxd2?? 38.Rxd2! e5? 39.Rxd6! you were suddenly winning, and you finished it off cleanly through 47.Rb8.

review.turning_point: 36...Rxc3?? by Black walked into 37.bxc3!, and the swing from about -4.9 to a winning position was complete after 39.Rxd6!.
review.focus: At 24.Qd5 you left a knight on b6 without enough protection. Before putting your queen on an active square, check every loose piece; 24.a4 was the safe, strong move.

review.headline: A well-played Giuoco Piano attack that collapsed in two moves

sections.text: You played a good Italian. The bishop trades on e3 and b3 were handled calmly, and 10.Nbd2 and 11.d4 were natural. After 17.e5 dxe5 18.Nxe5 Qb5 19.Qg3 you were building pressure on the king.

Black's 19...Ng6 allowed 20.Nxg6, and after 20...Rxe1+ 21.Rxe1 fxg6 you grabbed a pawn with 22.Qxc7. With 23.Re7 your rook sat on the seventh rank, and at +3.7 after 23...Nh5 you were close to winning.

Then 24.g4?? was the mistake. It was meant to chase the knight, but it weakened your king, and after 24...Qg5 the pawn on g4 was loose. The engine suggested 24.Qc4+, which kept the initiative with check.
25.Re2?? was worse. The rook retreated, but 25...Qxg4+ came with check and 26.Kh1 Qxe2 took the rook, so you resigned.

review.turning_point: 24.g4?? took you from +3.7 to -0.8, and 25.Re2?? after 24...Qg5 finished the game.
review.focus: At 24.g4 you played a pawn move that left the king exposed when a forcing check, 24.Qc4+, was available. When you are winning, look for checks before any pawn move.

review.headline: A messy Franco-Sicilian where both sides erred, and you converted until the clock ended it

sections.text: Black's 3...e6? and 4...Nge7?? gave you an early edge, though 4.Bc4?? was a missed chance for the stronger 4.d5. After 5.O-O? g6? 6.Re1 Bg7 7.Be3 O-O you were still fine, and 8.dxc5 won a pawn back for the structure.

After that you built up a large edge, +3.1 around 11...Qc7 and up to +4.6 after 15...Bf6. But 17.Rde1?? drifted, and 18.e5?? was the real blunder: 18...dxc4 left your bishop gone. The engine wanted 18.cxd6.

You fought back. 20.Nxe5! was the best move after 19...Bxe5, and Black's 20...f5?? brought you back to +5. Then 22.Qf6?? and 23.Nb5?? gave away the chance, but after 24.Qxf7+ Kxf7 25.Nd6+ you forked king and bishop, and Black's 25...Rxd6 26.cxd6 left you in a good position.
27.Rxe5! and 28.c3! showed good calculation, and 30.Rxe6+ cleaned up. You were up a huge amount of material when the opponent ran out of time on move 49.

review.turning_point: 18.e5?? dropped a bishop and made things difficult, but 20.Nxe5! restored the balance and 27.Rxe5! started the conversion.
review.focus: 18.e5 pushed a pawn when 18.cxd6 was better. Before advancing in the centre, check whether the pieces behind it, like your bishop on c4, are protected.

review.headline: A sharp Italian where your calculation in the opening won the game and a late slip nearly undid it

sections.text: You met 6...Bb4+ with 7.Nc3 and Black took 7...Nxe4 8.O-O Nxc3. Black then made the key mistake with 9...Ne7??, and you found the best reply, 10.bxc3!, followed by 11.Qb3.

Black snatched the rook with 11...Bxa1, and your 12.Bxf7+! was the idea behind it: after 12...Kf8 13.Bg5 d5 14.Bxe7+ Qxe7 15.Rxe7 Kxe7 you were attacking the exposed king, and 16.Qxd5 kept the initiative.

The only slip came at 17.Qe6+??, which dropped the evaluation from +5.5 to -8.3 since 17...Bxe6 simply took the queen. The engine pointed out 17.Qg5+ as the correct check. Luckily, Black played 17...Kf8?? and you were back to +3.1.
From there you were accurate. 18.Qc4! attacked the c7 pawn, 19.Qxc7 and 20.Ne5 brought more pieces in, and after 21.Bxe8 Rxe8 you finished with 22.Qf7#.

review.turning_point: 10.bxc3! after Black's 9...Ne7?? turned the opening around, and 12.Bxf7+! kept the king exposed.
review.focus: At 17.Qe6+ you checked without looking at whether the queen could be captured. 17.Qg5+ was safe. Before every check, ask whether the checking piece can simply be taken.

review.headline: A Petrov where White's errors gave you a big edge, but a few slips and a time crunch let it go

sections.text: You played the Petrov with 4...Nxe4 and 5...Qe7, and the opening was fairly equal. White's 11.Nb1?? and 12.b3? were mistakes, and your reply 12...a4! was the right way to go after the queenside. After 13.c4 axb3 14.axb3 Ra1 you were up to +3.4.

But 15...Nfd7?? gave it back. It opened a diagonal for 15.Bd4, and after 16.Bxa1 Bxa1 you were left worse. White then returned the favour with 17.Rd2?? and 18.Ra2??, and your 18...Bg7! was a good reply.

Another turning point came with 20...Bf5??, which dropped you to -1.1. White replied 21.d4??, and the best move was 21...Nd3+. 21...Qxe2 let White off the hook. After that it became a long, even fight with 25...Nxf2? and 27...Be3?.
You found 32...fxg3! and 34...Bf2!, but 33...Rg8?? was a lapse, and by 44...Kg7?? you were low on time. The engine wanted 44...Rxh3, and you lost on move 44.

review.turning_point: 21...Qxe2 let go of a position at +4.7, after White's 21.d4??; the strong follow-up was 21...Nd3+.
review.focus: At 21...Qxe2 you traded queens when 21...Nd3+ kept White tied up. When you are clearly ahead, look for the forcing move rather than the simplest exchange.

review.headline: A quick Philidor miniature where one careless reply let you take over

sections.text: You went for the Italian-style setup with 3.Bc4, and Black developed the bishop with 3...Bg4. Your 4.h3 Bh5 5.Nc3 forced a decision, and after 5...Bxf3 6.Qxf3 you had the bishop pair and the initiative.
7.g4?! was ambitious, and 7.a3 was the safer move. It was risky, but Black replied 7...c6??, which jumped the evaluation to +4.2. The better reply was 7...Nc6.
You punished it perfectly. 8.g5! kicked the knight, and after 8...d5 9.exd5 cxd5 10.Nxd5 Nxd5 11.Bxd5 you were a pawn up with a strong bishop. 12.Bxb7 made it two pawns.
Black resigned after that. It was a clean, quick win, and your accuracy of 93 reflects it.

review.turning_point: 8.g5! hit the knight right after Black's 7...c6??, and the exchanges that followed left you with the extra pawns.
review.focus: 7.g4 worked this time, but it weakened your kingside while your king was still uncastled. 7.a3 was safer; before a flank pawn push, check that your king is safe.

review.headline: A long game where you had a winning position several times and eventually lost on time

sections.text: White opened with 2.g3 and you answered with a sensible set-up: 3...d6, 4...Nc6 and 8...O-O. White's 10.O-O-O? gave you chances, but your 10...Bg4? and 11...d5?? let it slip, and 12.h3?? Bh5?? was another mix-up.

The first big moment was 19...Nb4?? (the engine wanted 19...a5), but White replied 20.Nc4??, and 20...Nxa2+! got you back into the game. After 21.Kb1 Bxb2 22.Kxb2 you were ahead, and 24...Nxd5! kept the advantage.
You built a big advantage: by 29.Rd1 you were at +5.3, and 36...a3+ and 37...Bxd1 kept you ahead. Time began to matter though, and 46...Kg8?? and 48...Ke7?? gave away tempo.

The endgame was a pawn race. You were winning at 64...h5, but 65...Kg4?? let White back in (65...h4 was the move), and 66...h4?? let White promote with 69.f8=Q. Finally 71...Kh3?? lost the position, and you ran out of time on move 76.

review.turning_point: 65...Kg4?? went from a forced win to -6.2 (65...h4 was the move), starting the sequence that led to the loss.
review.focus: Your clock decided this game. By 48...Ke7 you were already low on time, and 65...Kg4 threw away a winning endgame. When you are ahead, spend your time on simple, forcing moves such as 65...h4.

review.headline: A Rousseau Gambit where you survived the opening but overpressed in the middlegame

sections.text: Black played the Rousseau Gambit with 3...f5. After 4.d3 Nf6 5.Nc3 fxe4, your 6.Nxe4? was a mistake; 6.dxe4 was better. Black replied 6...Nxe4?? and you found the right recapture with 7.dxe4!.
7...d6? gave you a slight edge, though 8.Qd5? was not the best, since 8.Ng5 kept more. Black played 8...Qd7 and 9.Ng5?! Nd4 10.O-O h6 11.Nf7 c6 kept things busy.

12.Qa5 Rh7 13.f4 b5 14.fxe5 bxc4 kept the game alive, with the knight on f7 deep in Black's camp. But 15.e6?? was the blunder, since 15...Nxe6 took the pawn and exposed the queen; 15.Be3 was the safer move.
After 16.Qh5 g6 17.Qxg6 Rxf7 the knight on f7 fell and you were well down in material, so you resigned.

review.turning_point: 15.e6?? turned a balanced attack into a lost position at -2.1; 15.Be3 would have kept the tension.
review.focus: At 15.e6 you pushed a pawn forward when your pieces were not ready. 15.Be3 developed your last piece. Before pushing a pawn in an attack, make sure the rest of your pieces are involved.

review.headline: A London System game where you survived a bishop sacrifice and then walked into a decisive attack

sections.text: You played the solid 1...d5 and 3...Bd6 against the London, and 5...Nh5 was an active choice. After 6.Bb5+ c6 7.Bd3 Nxg3 8.fxg3 O-O you had traded off White's dark-squared bishop and the position was fine.
White's 9.h4?? was an overreach, and 9...c5?! was not the strongest answer. 10.Bxh7+? was a sacrifice that White could not afford, and you answered correctly with 10...Kxh7!, taking the bishop.

11.Ng5+ was the critical moment. 11...Kg8?? moved the king back onto the file where White's queen could arrive, and the evaluation fell from +2.9 to -9.5. 11...Kh6 was the move, followed by 12.Nc3 g6.
After 12.Qh5 Bxg3+ 13.Ke2 Qxg5 14.hxg5 f6 15.g6 you were lost, and you resigned.

review.turning_point: 11...Kg8?? swung the game from +2.9 to -9.5, after you had played the sacrifice perfectly with 10...Kxh7!.
review.focus: At 11...Kg8 you had two king moves after the check, and the wrong one allowed 12.Qh5. When your king takes a sacrifice, check where the opponent's queen can go next; 11...Kh6 was the move.

review.headline: A Paris Defence where Black grabbed a poisoned pawn, and you converted a queen trap into a mating attack

sections.text: Black played 4...Bg4 and you took the pawn with 5.dxe5?!. 5.h3 was a little more accurate. After 5...Nxe5 6.Be2 Nxf3+ 7.Bxf3 Bxf3 8.Qxf3 Qf6 you had a small edge with a pleasant position.
You developed with 9.Qd3, 10.O-O, 11.Nc3 and 12.Nd5, and Black pushed with 10...h5 and 11...h4. Then 13.Bf4 set a trap: 13...Qxb2?? grabbed the pawn, and 14.Rfb1! was the best reply.
After 14...Qxa1 15.Rxa1 you gave a rook for the queen and were up around +5.6. 16.Nxf6 gxf6 and 17.Be3 kept the pressure on, and 18.Bxa7 picked up another pawn.
22.Bxb6! was a sharp shot, with the c7 pawn pinned against the rook on d8. 24.Ba5?! was slightly loose (24.a4 was cleaner), but you finished well. 29.Qxg8 took a rook, and 41.Qa8# ended it.

review.turning_point: 14.Rfb1! trapped the queen after 13...Qxb2??, and after 15.Rxa1 you were up a queen for a rook.
review.focus: At 24.Ba5?! you gave back about two pawns of advantage (+5.5 to +3.7). 24.a4 kept everything under control. When you are winning, keep your moves simple.

review.headline: A Petrov where you fell behind early, then punished a kingside attack that went too far

sections.text: 3...Bc5?? against the Italian setup was a mistake, since 4.Nxe5 took a pawn for free. The engine suggested 3...Nxe4 instead. After 5.d4 Bd6? 6.Nc3 Nc6? you were around -3.8, and 7.Nxc6 dxc6 left you without much.
White's 8.Bg5? was a mistake, since 8.e5 was stronger, and you got breathing room. After 10.O-O Nd5 11.Bxe7 Rxe7 12.Nxd5 cxd5 you were still behind, but the position was easier to play.

White pushed ahead with 14.Qh5, 15.Qh6 and 16.h4, but 19.h5? was too hasty, and you snapped up a pawn with 19...Qxc2?!. The real error was 22.f4??, which jumped the evaluation to +3.4 for you. Your reply 22...Rf5! pinned the f4 pawn against the rook on f1 and set up the queen trade.
After 23.Qh3 Rh5 24.Qxh5 gxh5 you picked up the queen for a rook, and 25...Qxb2 and 26...Qxd4 brought more. You finished with 30...Qg4#.

review.turning_point: 22.f4?? by White, met with 22...Rf5!, turned a lost position into a winning one.
review.focus: At 3...Bc5 you allowed 4.Nxe5. In the Petrov, if White plays 3.Bc4, 3...Nxe4 is the way to keep material level.

review.headline: A calm Giuoco Pianissimo where one pawn push punished a careless bishop move

sections.text: You played the Italian patiently: 4.d3, 5.Be3, and after 5...Bxe3 6.fxe3 O-O you had an open f-file and a solid centre. 7.h3 and 8.Nc3 were sensible, and 9.O-O completed development.

10.d4 challenged the centre, and Black's 10...Be6?? was a mistake, jumping the evaluation to +3.6 (10...Nxe4 11.Nxe4 was the engine's choice). You found 11.d5!, which forked the knight on c6 and the bishop on e6.
11...Nb4 12.dxe6 fxe6 13.a3 Nc6 14.Bxe6+ left you ahead by the equivalent of a piece, with a very safe king. 15.Nd5 Nxd5 16.Bxd5 simplified further, and Black resigned.
A clean game: accuracy 95.7 with no errors. You kept control, avoided risks and punished the first real mistake.

review.turning_point: 11.d5! forked the knight and bishop after Black's 10...Be6??, and the extra material was never in doubt.
review.focus: No errors to point at. For practice, look at 10...Nxe4 11.Nxe4, which the engine preferred for Black, and think about how you would keep your edge in that line.

review.headline: A Petrov where a rook-lift mix-up gave you the initiative and you finished with a strong queen move

sections.text: You played the Petrov carefully: 4...Nxe4 5.Qe2 Qe7 6.d3 Nf6 7.Be3 Bg4. White tried 10.g4 and 11.Nc4, and your 11...Nd5 and 12...Nxe3 13.fxe3 gave you a safe position with castling long on 13...O-O-O.
White played 15.Na5 and 16.O-O-O, then 17.b4? was a mistake (17.Nab3 was better). You replied 17...b6??, which swung the evaluation to -2.4 after 18.Naxc6. 17...d5 was the move to play.
After 18...Nxc6 19.Nxc6 you played 19...Re8?, when 19...d5 was stronger. White had the edge, but 20.Nd4? let you in, and 20...d5! was the right idea.
21.Rhf1?? was the decisive mistake. You took 21...Bxb4, and after 22.Bxd5?? the move 22...Qc3! pinned the c2 pawn against the king on c1 and White resigned after 23.Nb3 Ba3+.

review.turning_point: 22...Qc3! after White's 21.Rhf1?? and 22.Bxd5??, which pinned the c2 pawn and left White defenceless.
review.focus: 17...b6 weakened your queenside when 17...d5 kept things simple. Before a quiet pawn move, check which pieces of yours it leaves loose, especially near your king.

review.headline: A tactical Caro-Kann slugfest where you chased chances, gave them back, and finally ran out of time

sections.text: This Caro-Kann Exchange became a wild blitz fight, and early on you were steering it. After fatpossum's 7...Bh5 you found the sharp reply 8.g4!, kicking the bishop around and reaching about +1.4.

The first slip was 9.Nh4. The engine wanted 9.Ne5, keeping the knight in the centre, and after 9...Be4 the evaluation fell to -0.7. Then 13.Bxf6 allowed 13...Qg3+, and after 14.Kd2 your king was stuck in the middle for the rest of the game.
