Your opponent gave you chances back. 16...Rxh3 was a blunder and 17.Rxh3 was the right answer. After 21...Qg3 you found 22.Qa6+ and 24.Qa5+, which set up a skewer on the king and the rook behind it and brought the game back to 0.0. In between, 23.c6 was a slip, since 23.Qb5+ kept the pressure.
Then 27.Rc1+ threw it away. The checking rook was simply captured by 27...Bxc1, and at -4.4 with the clock draining, the rest was damage limitation until your flag fell.

review.turning_point: 27.Rc1+ swung the game from +0.3 to -4.1, because the bishop on h6 could just take the rook. 27.Qc8+ kept the balance.
review.focus: Before you play a check, ask what can capture the checking piece, as with 27.Rc1+ Bxc1. Also notice that 9.Nh4 left the knight offside when 9.Ne5 was available.

review.headline: A messy Vienna where you survived early slips, won a piece, and finished with a back rank mate

sections.text: Against the Vienna you pinned the knight early with 3...Bg4, but it did not bring much. 5...Qd7 missed the better 5...Bxf3, and White settled into a comfortable game at -1.9 for you.

8...Bxf3 dropped to -3.2 when 8...dxe5 was better. Luckily 9.Bxf3 was a blunder by White (9.exf6 was the move), and you found 9...Bxe5 to get back to about -0.2. After 12...Bxc3 13.bxc3 Qc6 14.Bf3 Qxc3 you had also picked up a pawn.
White's 18.d7 and especially 19.Bf3 turned the game. You found 19...Nd4!, and after 20.Qb1 Nxf3+ you had won a piece. After 22...Rxd7 and the rook trade on d3 you were well ahead at +4 or more.

Your conversion wobbled. 27...Qd4 gave some back, and 31...Qxg3 dropped the evaluation from +5.0 to 0.0, as White got checks on e5 and e4. After 34...Kc8 you were objectively lost, but 35.Rxa7 walked into 35...Rd1+! and the back rank mate.

review.turning_point: 35...Rd1+ was a back rank shot that ended the game after White grabbed the pawn with 35.Rxa7 instead of playing 35.Rc1+.
review.focus: With a big lead, check what the opponent's checks lead to. 31...Qxg3 grabbed a pawn when 31...Qd4 kept everything under control.

review.headline: A scrappy Philidor-style game won on the clock after both sides traded blunders

sections.text: You went for a solid setup after 2.Bc4 d6 and traded bishops with 4.Bxe6 fxe6. The pawn break 8...d5 gave White the better chances at -1.5, but 10.Bd2 was a slip (10.d4 was better) and you found the good reply 10...Nf6!.

White kept up pressure with 14.Rhe1 and 15.Nf5, but 16.Ng3 let you off, since 16.Nxd6+ was stronger. Your tactical moment came at 19...Qxf2: after 20.Qxf2 Nxf2! the queens came off and you were a pawn up.

Both sides then swapped errors. 29...h5 was a blunder (29...Rf4 was needed), but 31.Rfxf2 gave it back and you found 31...Rxf2. 33...Rh5 let White back in, 34.Nf1 returned the favour and you answered with 34...g5!.
In the ending 37.Ne7 gave you +4.2, but 37...c6 threw it away; 37...g4 was the move. In time trouble 42...Rf1 and 44...Rg2 followed. After 45.Rxg2 hxg2 you were worse, but White's flag fell first.

review.turning_point: 37...c6 let a +4.2 position slide back to 0.0, when 37...g4 kept your edge.
review.focus: Under time pressure, look for forcing moves first, as with 37...g4 and 29...Rf4, rather than quiet pawn moves like 29...h5 that leave tactics behind.

review.headline: A Jerome Gambit that backfired, a long fight back, and a drawn ending lost on the clock

sections.text: You went for the Jerome Gambit with 4.Bxf7+, and the engine did not like it at -2.8; 4.c3 was the sound move. After 4...Kxf7 5.Nxe5+ Nxe5 6.Qh5+ Ng6 7.Qxc5 you had dragged the king out but were still at -2.4.
IronEagleBird made errors too. 12...Ng4 and 13...Bd7 gave you +2.1, but 14.Qh5 wasted it (14.Qc4+ was better), and 17.Bh4 simply lost a piece to 17...Nxh4, taking you to -5.4.

You kept fighting. 29...Qxh2+ 30.Kxh2! traded queens, and 33.Rg7+! set up a skewer on the king and the bishop on d7. Black answered 34...Rh8+ and later 41...Rd8, and your 40.e5! and 42.e6! brought you to +4.5.
Then the clock hurt you. 43.exd7 gave the win away (43.Rxd7+ was clear), 45.Kf2 was another slip (45.a4 kept the edge), and in the pawn ending 57.Kc2 lost where 57.a3 held.

review.turning_point: 43.exd7 fell from +4.5 to +0.1 when 43.Rxd7+ Rxd7 44.exd7 Kxd7 45.a4 kept a clear advantage.
review.focus: At 43.exd7 you picked the natural recapture and missed the forcing 43.Rxd7+. When you are winning, spend your time on the forcing line first.

review.headline: A Queen's Gambit Declined where you rode out early slips and White gave you a piece

sections.text: Against the London-style 3.Bf4 you played the Queen's Gambit Declined. After 4.Bxd6 you recaptured 4...cxd6, but 4...Qxd6 was better, and White had a small edge at -1.3.

The real mistake came at 10...Qb6, where 10...Nxc3 was the right idea. White answered with 11.Qa4, which missed 11.Nxd5, and then 11...Qc6 put your queen in front of the rook on e8 on the same diagonal as the queen on a4. 11...Bd7 was safer.

That was your lucky escape: 12.Qxc6 was another White error (12.Bb5 was better), and 12...bxc6! traded queens and left you only slightly worse at -0.6. After that you slowly improved your pieces with 13...Bg4, 15...Be6 and 16...Bf5. 17...Bg6 gave a little back, since 17...Nxc3 was better.
The decisive moment was 20.Bxe4, which swung the evaluation to +3.7. 20...Rxe4! won a piece, and you converted calmly with 22...c5 and 24...Rb8 until White resigned after 30...Nxa2.

review.turning_point: 20.Bxe4 was White's blunder, and 20...Rxe4! won a piece and swung the evaluation to +3.7.
review.focus: Look at 10...Qb6: 10...Nxc3 won a piece or more. Before you play a queen move, check whether a capture on the board wins material.

review.headline: A clean attacking win where one check led to a piece and then to mate

sections.text: A model game for you, accuracy 96. After 3.Bc4 Be7 you played 4.d4 and recaptured with 5.Nxd4, putting a knight on d4 in the centre. Black wandered with 5...Ne5, and 6.Bb3 followed by 8.f4 chased the knight back and gave you the space.
After 9.Re1 and 10.Qd3 you were ready to strike. Black's 10...Nb4 (the engine preferred 10...Nxd4) set up your moment: 11.Qb5+! forked the king on e8 and the knight on b4.
12.Qxb4 won the knight, and you were suddenly a piece up at +2.5. Black tried 12...c5, hoping to chase the queen, but 13.Qc4 kept the queen safe and aimed with the bishop on b3 at f7.
13...cxd4 was the last mistake, and the engine says it lost by force. 14.Qxf7# finished it. Black's king had no way out because the bishop on e7 and the queen on d8 were blocking its own escape.

review.turning_point: 11.Qb5+ forked the king and the knight on b4, winning a piece and setting up the mate on f7.
review.focus: Keep hunting for forcing checks that hit two things at once, as 11.Qb5+ did here. Your play was clean, so the habit to keep is looking at every check before you play slowly.

review.headline: A Philidor where a strong start slipped away through loose queen moves and a final rook sacrifice that did not work

sections.text: You played the open 4.d4 against the Philidor and had a nice position, especially after 7...Be6, which was a blunder by Black (7...Bd7 was better). The engine gave you +3.2, and 8.Nxe6 fxe6 9.Bxe6 would have won a pawn.

Instead 8.Bb3 Bxb3 9.axb3 gave away the bishop pair and your evaluation fell to +1.0. You still got chances when Black played 13...g5. After 14.f4 Ng4 you needed 15.Nf5, but 15.fxg5 let Black back in with 15...Nxe3 16.Qxe3.

You then found a strong idea with 17.Nf5!, which pointed at g7 and brought you back to +2.6. 18.Nxg7 Kxg7 19.Rf5 kept the pressure, but 21.Qf3 was inaccurate (21.Qd4 kept +2.8) and you let Black untangle with 21...Ne5.
24.Qd5 was the final blunder, where 24.Qd3 held. 24...Ne3 hit your queen, and 25.Rxg5+ fxg5 simply lost material. White's Black pieces hold; you resigned at -3.6.

review.turning_point: 24.Qd5 dropped from +2.8 to 0.0 and 25.Rxg5+ then lost material; 25.Qxb7+ would have kept the balance.
review.focus: At 8.Bb3 you gave up the bishop pair when 8.Nxe6 fxe6 9.Bxe6 was ahead. Check forcing captures before retreating.

review.headline: A calm Bishop's Opening where you were fine until a missed fork and a last-move blunder

sections.text: Against the Bishop's Opening you played ...d6 and ...Be6, and after 4.Bxe6 fxe6 you had a solid if slightly passive structure. 6...c6 and 7...Be7 were small inaccuracies, but 9.dxe5 Nxe5 10.Nxe5 dxe5 traded off the central tension and left you only slightly worse.
The key moment came at 13.Na4, a mistake by White. The engine liked 13...Qb5, a fork of the knight on a4 and the queen on e2. Instead you played 13...Qa5, and the evaluation sank to -0.6.
You kept your composure. After 17...Bc5 18.Bxc5 Qxc5 you were back to about -0.6, and 20...Qxe4 21.Qxe4 Nxe4 22.Nxe6 Rxf2 simplified into an equal endgame at 0.0.
The end came at 23...Nd2. 23...Rf6 was the move, and instead 24.Kxf2 simply took your rook. After that the position was at -5.8 and you resigned.

review.turning_point: 23...Nd2 turned an equal position into -5.8, since 24.Kxf2 took the rook that had just been left on f2.
review.focus: Before a move that looks forcing, such as 23...Nd2, check whether your own pieces on f2 and e4 stay protected. Also look for forks first, like 13...Qb5.

review.headline: A Center Game where a big early gift was missed, then a time-trouble loss

sections.text: White opened with the Center Game, and the early queen move 4.Qc3 was a blunder. 4...Bb4 would have pinned the queen on c3 to the king and given you +5.1. You played 4...d6 instead, and the advantage disappeared, down to -0.1.

You then played a solid middlegame, with 5...Bd7, 7...Be7 and 8...O-O, and after 11.Bxc6 Bxc6 you were fine. White overpressed with 15.h5 and 16.exd5, and you found 15...d5! and 16...Nxd5!, getting to +4.2.

17...Bb4 was the next error, where 17...Bxc4 was best. After 18.Qxd5, 18...Rxe2 was a blunder (18...Qxd5 was better), and 19.Qxd8+ made it -5.3. From there White simply traded down and queened a pawn.
The rest was a lost ending, and you flagged on move 56.

review.turning_point: 18...Rxe2 turned a good position at +1.4 into -5.1, because 19.Qxd8+ won the queen. 18...Qxd5 was the move.
review.focus: On 4.Qc3 you had a strong shot, the 4...Bb4 pin, and missed it. When the opponent's queen is out early, check for pins first.

review.headline: A winning Black gift squandered in time trouble and ended in mate

sections.text: Black opened with 2...Qf6, and you found the best reply 3.Nc3! to take advantage. After 4.d4 Bd6 5.Bg5 Qg6 you had a large edge, and 6.dxe5 Bxe5 7.Qd2 kept it.

A small slip came with 9.Be2 and 10.Be3, and you got into a long maneuvering phase. 14.Rhe1! pinned the knight on e7 against the rook on e8 and took you to +4.9. But 15.Re3 let some of the advantage go (15.Bd6 was better).
17.Bc4 Rxe3 18.fxe3 was fine, and Black's 18...b5 was a mistake, which gave you +6.1. Then 19.Bb3 Bb7 20.Qd3 Qxg2 started letting the attack flow to your king.
21.Qxh7 was the mistake, played low on time, because it left the knight on f3 to be won by 21...Qxf3. 22.Rg1 was the final blunder, and 23.Kb1 Qxg1# finished the game.

review.turning_point: 22.Rg1 turned a still-manageable position into -6.0; 22.e4 was the right defence, and 23...Qxg1# followed.
review.focus: With a big lead, slow down and check your king. 22.Rg1 and 21.Qxh7 were played low on time, while 22.e4 covered everything.

review.headline: A Sicilian where you kept finding good ideas and then missing the simple capture on c6

sections.text: You played the open Sicilian against the Accelerated Dragon, and 5.Bc4 and 6.Be3 were normal. 8.Qd2 and 9.O-O-O set up the Yugoslav-style attack, and 10.Bh6 was thematic.
11.h3 was the first slip, where 11.Bxg7 was needed. Black gave it back immediately with 11...b5, and the sequence 12.Nd5 Nxd5 13.Bxg7 Kxg7 14.Bxd5 gave you +1.9. Black's 14...Bb7 made it +4.3.
That was the moment: 15.Nxc6 was the move, and instead 15.h4 threw the advantage away (+0.1). 15...h5 and 16.g4 repeated the pattern, as 16.Nxc6 was again stronger, and 17.Qf4 missed 17.Nxc6.
After 17...e6 18.Bxe6 you were close to equal. 20.Qxd6 then simplified into an ending at -4.0, where 20.Rxd6 was the correct recapture. You flagged on move 34.

review.turning_point: 15.h4 threw away a +4.3 position (down to +0.1), when 15.Nxc6 b4 16.Nxb4 kept the advantage.
review.focus: At 15.h4, 16.g4 and 17.Qf4 the same idea, 15.Nxc6, was available three times. When the opponent leaves a piece pinned or attacked, take it before starting your own plan.

review.headline: A King's Gambit Declined where the opponent walked into a tactical net and you collected material

sections.text: Against the King's Gambit Declined you played 2...Nc6 and then 3...Nf6, which the engine liked less than 3...exf4. But 4.d4 was a blunder by White, and you found 4...exd4! at once.
5.Nxd4 was another error (5.e5 was better), and you replied with 5...Nxe4!. After 6.Nxc6 bxc6 7.Bd3 you struck: 7...Qh4+! pinned the pawn on h2 against the rook on h1.
8...Nxg3! was a lovely follow-up, a best move that puts a piece en prise. After 9.Kd2 Nxh1 you had won the exchange and more, with the material count at +7.

You converted without any hurry: 10...Qxf4+, 11...Qe5+ and 13...Qxh2+ kept White's king under pressure. After 14.Qf2 Qxf2+ and the bishop trade you were up a lot of material, and White resigned after 31...Re8.

review.turning_point: 7...Qh4+ and 8...Nxg3! won the rook on h1 and turned an equal position into +4.8.
review.focus: 3...Nf6 allowed 4.d4, which was a blunder, but 3...exf4 was better. In the King's Gambit, take the pawn when you can.

review.headline: A short Italian where you were doing well, and the game ended with your resignation

sections.text: You played the Italian with 4.c3 and 5.d4, a standard central plan. After 5...exd4 6.Bg5 Qg6, Black's queen was out early, and you used it.

7...h6 was a mistake by Black (7...d6 was better), and you found 8.Bh4!, which kept the bishop on the diagonal. After 8...dxc3 9.Nxc3 d6 10.Nd5 Bb6 you had lots of development and attacking chances at +2.5.

11...Bh3 was another mistake by Black. The engine says 12.Nf4 was best, a fork of the queen on g6 and the bishop on h3. You played 12.Bg3 instead, which was only an inaccuracy and still left you at +2.8.
The engine had you better when the game ended. The result is recorded as a loss by resignation after 12.Bg3 Bg4, so I would look at why you resigned in a position rated about +3.5 in your favour.

review.turning_point: 11...Bh3 gave you the chance for 12.Nf4, forking the queen and the bishop; the game ended instead with your resignation.
review.focus: At 12.Bg3 look first for forcing options like 12.Nf4. Do not resign a position like this: check the material and the threats before you give up.

review.headline: A Colle-style game where one rook slip nearly cost you, and the opponent's blunder gave you the win

sections.text: You played a flexible Queen's Pawn setup and equalised easily with 6...c5 and 8...Qxd5. After the queens came off with 9.Qxd5 Nxd5 the game was balanced, though 15...b5 and 17...Bb7 were small inaccuracies.

Moein_doozande got the upper hand at 20.Nd7, which uncovered an attack from the bishop on b2 on your bishop on f6 and threatened your rook on f8. 20...Rfd8 was a blunder, while 20...Bxb2 was the move.
You were down to -3.1, but you kept playing. 21.Nxf6+ Nxf6 22.Rxd8+ Rxd8 23.Bxf6 gxf6 simplified, and White's 24.g3 was a mistake, which you punished with 24...Rd2!.

Your active rook and bishop caused problems: 25.Bf1 Ra2 26.Rb3 Ra1 and the decisive 29.Rb3 was a blunder by White. You found 29...Be2!, and 30.Kg2 Bxf1+ won the bishop. From there 37...Bxh5 and 41...Rh1# finished the job.

review.turning_point: 29.Rb3 was White's blunder, and 29...Be2! won a bishop and swung the game from +0.4 to +4.1.
review.focus: At 20...Rfd8 the right move was 20...Bxb2, which took the attacking bishop first. When your opponent makes a discovered attack, check what the uncovered piece is really hitting.

review.headline: An Owen Defense full of swings that ended in time trouble

sections.text: You played the Owen Defense with 1...b6, and White got a comfortable edge. After 5...Bb4 6.Bd2 Bxc3 7.Bxc3 d5 you reached a normal position. White's 13.Bb4 attacked your queen but allowed 13...Nxb4!.
You were fine after that, but 19.Ba4 (19.Re3 was better) and 20.c3 were White's mistakes. You missed them: 19...Rad8 and 20...a6 both let the advantage go. 19...Ba6 was the way to profit.
The game kept swinging. 28.Nc6 opened the e-file against your rook and 29...Nxg2 was a blunder (29...h4 was needed), but 30.Qxg2 returned the favour and you found 30...Qxc6!, winning a piece.
You were winning, but low on time 37...a3 dropped to -4.1 (37...Qa3 was best), and 41...Qbc1 allowed a forced mate (41...Qaa2 was the move). The game ended on the clock.

review.turning_point: 37...a3 swung the evaluation from +0.8 to -4.1; 37...Qa3 would have kept the extra material.
review.focus: Late in the game, watch your clock and your pieces' safety together, as with 37...a3 and 41...Qbc1. Simple checks and queen safety beat pawn pushes.

review.headline: A smooth Old Indian Attack where you punished one central push and converted with care

sections.text: You met the Zukertort set-up with a solid ...d5 and ...e6 plan. 7...b6 was only a small inaccuracy (7...h6 was a shade better). White's 8.e4 Bb7 then led to the key moment.
9.e5 forked the bishop on d6 and the knight on f6, but it was a blunder, because you replied 9...Nxe5! 10.Nxe5 Bxe5. With the pair of pieces developed you were a pawn up, +1.7.

11...Bxc3 slightly relaxed (11...Bd6 was a shade better). After 12.bxc3 and 13.Bxf6 Qxf6 you kept control, with 14...Rad8 and 15...Bxd5 coordinating your rooks and queen. Your edge grew slowly to +3.6.

23...Ra5 and 24...Qc5 were small inaccuracies, but 26...Qxa2 27.Qxa2 Rxa2 left you two pawns up in the endgame. 29...Rxc4 30.dxe6 Rxd1 31.exf7+ Kxf7 32.Rxd1 and 34.Rxc7 Rxc7 left you with a winning ending. White resigned.

review.turning_point: 9.e5 was a blunder, and 9...Nxe5! turned a calm position into a clear +1.8 for you.
review.focus: Your play was accurate. The small points were 7...b6 and 11...Bxc3; ask whether a move like 7...h6 would have kept the position simpler.

review.headline: A Scandinavian gambit where a good start collapsed into dropped pieces

sections.text: You went for the Boehnke Gambit-style line with 2.exd5 e6 3.dxe6 Bxe6 and developed naturally with 4.Nf3, 5.Be2 and 6.O-O. The engine rated you well, at +2.1 to +2.8.
9.h3 was a slightly loose move, and 10.Bxc6 bxc6 11.d4 Qd6 took the pressure out. 12.g3 was a mistake, as 12.Nc3 kept more of the edge and it dropped you from +3.1 to +1.6.
14.hxg4 was a blunder, where 14.Nc3 was needed. 15.Nh2 then left a piece to be won; the engine wanted 15.Nh4. Black missed 15...Rxh2 and played 15...Qf5, which gave you a chance to escape.
Instead 16.Qxg4 lost your queen to 16...Qxg4, and you resigned. 16.Re5 was the only move.

review.turning_point: 16.Qxg4 walked into 16...Qxg4 and lost the queen, turning a position at -0.6 into -6.5.
review.focus: At 14.hxg4 you captured a pawn with your king exposed. Before grabbing material, check whether 14.Nc3 develops and keeps your pieces protected.

review.headline: A Petrov where a pawn storm met an overextended Black position and you resigned from near equality

sections.text: You played the Three Knights Petrov with 2...Nf6, and White chose 4.h3. 4...Be6 was a little awkward at -1.3, and 5.d3 was a slip by White, but you did not take the advantage. 7.g4 and 8.g5 started a pawn storm.
After 11.exd5 cxd5 12.Bxb6 axb6 the structure was healthy but you were behind. 13.h4 was strong, and 13...Bg4 was a blunder, since 13...b5 was the move.
White then went wrong with 14.O-O and 15.Qd2. You answered with 14...Nc5 and 15...e4, but both were mistakes: 14...d4 and 15...d4 were better. Even so you reached about -0.5.

21.g6 was strong, but 21...Bxh4 was a mistake (21...O-O was the move), and after 22.gxf7+ Bxf7 you were slightly worse. The engine rated the final position close to level, so the resignation after 26.Ne2 looks premature.

review.turning_point: 13...Bg4 wasted your good position, dropping from +1.4 to -0.3.
review.focus: At 13...Bg4 you spent a move on a bishop that White could attack. 13...b5 improved your queenside instead. Check what your opponent's pawn storm can kick before you move.

review.headline: A topsy-turvy game you won by punishing a queen blunder and a final queen swap

sections.text: White opened with the Van't Kruijs 1.e3 and then 2.Qh5, a mistake that you did not punish. 2...d6 was a little passive, and White built up with 3.Bb5+ c6 4.Bc4 g6 5.Qf3.

8...Bxe2 was a mistake (8...Be6 was better), and White returned the favour with 9.Ngxe2. 9.Qxe5+ was the right move. You played well in the middlegame with 12.fxe5 Bxe5 13.d4 Bd6, and then went wrong with 15...Be7 and 16...Qa6, which dropped to -2.0.
17.Qe1 was a blunder, and you found 17...Bxb4!, which pinned the knight on c3 to the queen. After 18.axb4 Qxa1 you had won material (+3).
19...cxb5 and 21...Nb6 were slips, but White's 21.Nbc3 and 22.Nf4 repaid you. You found 22...Nc4!, and 24.Qxf6 Qxf6! left you a queen up. White resigned.

review.turning_point: 17...Bxb4! pinned the knight on c3 to the queen and won material after White's blunder 17.Qe1.
review.focus: At 21...Nb6 you left a piece to be won; 21...Rhe8 was safe. Check what a knight move leaves undefended before you play it.
